question: GOD is perfect, then how about his creation, is it perfect?
answer:
Imperfection is perfection.

Perfection is God makes more sense than saying that God is Perfect. God for people is simply a perfect state of mind. Whatever appears to be perfect state of mind, people just assume that it's God.

When it comes to the creation, yes if it feels perfect, it must be perfect. Perfection of the creation once again depends on people's state of mind. In some situations, even if everything is perfect, people don't feel it's perfect because of their of own personality and attitude (state of mind). For example, for some people a long nose might look perfect on someone but the one with long nose may not think it looks good. Perfection depends on how self-confident you are.

question: GOD is perfect, then how about his creation, is it perfect?
answer:
> hello brothers and sisters,
>                                        sat sri akal. if GOD is perfect, then how about his creation, is it perfect or full of defects? is it necessary for us to remodify our bodies, like cutting body parts, cutting nose, cutting ears and so on, in the path of spirituality?  or is man already been created in a perfect manner, no modification is needed in the path of spirituality? if at all  there are defects then where they are located, in the body, or in the mind-thoughts? so should i rectify the body or mind?  thank you very much

Sat Sri Akaal,

God can be nothing if not 'perfect' -- so the attempt to formulate a logical 'cause-effect' link of 'perfection' from Creator to Creation is an exercise in irrelevance.  All the universe is exactly as it should be, as this is how is was designed.

When you talk about the necessity of such and such spiritual custom, it's entirely subjective  -- as we acknowledge that there are many paths to God... Sikhi being one of if not the greatest (in my humble and wholly subjective and biased opinion!) and each 'path' has evolved it's own customs and requisites, then the necessity of 'modifying' our bodies can be understood, even if we disapprove. For example, the analogy I'd make, although it takes some imagination, is the Dastaar. Not simply fabric, nor simply 'Head Gear', but don't we consider Dastaar, or Turban, to be more than symbolic: Don't many Khalsa consider Dastaar to be an actual physical structure of their head -- in effect, a 'modification' of their physical bodies for spiritual purpose? And I should add, are they not correct?? I believe they are! Please correct me if I am wrong ..

I don't believe we should dwell on the concept of perfection as relates to any of God's creations. If we were created 'perfect', then God wouldn't be so special.

 Also, semantically,  it all depends on how you define 'perfection'.

question: GOD is perfect, then how about his creation, is it perfect?
answer:
[member],

There is only ONE entity that is truly Perfect,and that is God,Almighty Waheguru.
Creation is His Maya,and Sikhism teaches that God is True(Sachaa) and His Creation is also True(Sachi).But Maya is not perfect.It  has imperfections.It is characterized by 3 gunas (rajo,tamo,sato or rajas,tamas,satvik).When we dwell on Maya the enchantress,she takes us away from God.

So we should try not to get tempted or carried away by Maya and its lures,and focus singlemindedly on God all the time.
A healthy mind in a healthy body with constant Remembrance of Waheguru,is the Sikh way or Guru's Way.

Your aim should be to restrain yourself from the 5 evils and follow the routine prescribed by the Gursikh lifestyle according to teachings of Sikhism.

Best wishes.

question: Simran through Kandh?
answer:
Everyone is right in a way. There is an old Indian saying, similar to “A bird in hand...." that goes “Paisa Gunth Bani Kunth” meaning that your money is only what you have in your possession and Bani is only what you have committed to your memory.

“Kunth” or “Kanth” (it sounds the same as ‘Hunt’ with a K) means neck (or throat.) It also means bosom in Gurbani. In colloquial Punjabi this word is used for memorizing something, derived from being able to recite something from your voice box (or memory) instead of reciting from a paper.

Some people describe Simran as “four” kinds. Of these the first two kinds (Madhma and Baikhari) could be considered to be throaty. Personally, I do not subscribe to any dissection of Simran.

question: Historical Dates - please verify
answer:
[member] ji,

Even though Sikhism is relatively young religion, establishing exact dates is still pretty challenging! One reason being the turmoil and destruction which Sikhs suffered pretty much throughout the history and lots of history and manuscripts are lost. Here is some information that I can share. Kartarpuri pothi is dated manuscript and according to Gurinder Singh Mann, who actually saw Kartarpuri bir, it has the date "Sammat 1661 miti Bhadon vadi ekam 1 pothi likh pahunche" inscribed on Folio 2 as date of completion(Gurinder Singh Mann, Making of Sikh Scripture, p.63). Which translates into 1 day after Poornmasi, of Bhaddon month in sammat 1661. Prof. Sahib Singh also gives the same date for completion of Adi Granth and date of First Parkash as Bhaddon Sudi 1, 1661. Prof. Paul Singh Purewal (man behind Nanakshahi Calendar) calculates that date to correspond to Sep. 1st, 1604 in Gregorian Calendar as the day of 1st Parkash of Adi Granth at Harimandir Sahib.

I am not sure if we can truly calculate how many years it took Guru Arjan Sahib to complete Adi Granth as earlier pothis (Guru harsahai, Goindval pothi) were already available.

As for Guruship to Granth Sahib, the one entry we read about is from Bhatt Narbud Singh, said to be an eyewitness. He records the date as , "satran sai painsath kartik mas ki chauth shukla pakkhe budhvar ke dihun" (considered Oct. 6, 1708). I have also heard Oct 20th as the "official date" recognized as the gurugaddi of Guru Granth Sahib.

Although I didn't live in a village, I used to go my mom's village so often that I established a bond with the people in the neighborhood. But now, it's been a while since I went there. A sore throat  and fever reminded me of reminding everyone who grew up in a village that they might be missing someone who is like a family member or actually more than family member. When I went to my mom's village, I used to get sick a lot. An old lady whom everybody referred to as chaachi would rub my throat and usually it felt better but if it didn't and I really couldn't walk to the doctor, a man I often referred to as maamaji would actually carry me to the doctor. I have been sick for last couple days and this is what reminded me of them as how close people in the village were to each other, just like family and these people were of different religion and caste.

I was a little kid. Maybe not many people remember me but I wanted to remind some of the people who grew up in villages and then settled out of India that there might someone there in your village who just might be as close as your family.

question: Do you ever look back at your village?
answer:
SSA Ji,

   Whenever my family and I go back to India, we always go back to Punjab, and my dads pind. I was born and raised in Canada, and only go back to India every 5-10 years. So in total, I've only gone back 3 times. Each time our visit to India usually consists of Delhi, and tourist locations. Whilst the tourist locations are heavenly, and the sites we visit are breath taking, whenever people ask me, so what did you like the most in India? I always say, dads pind. Every time I've got holidays from uni, my parents ask me where do you want to go, and guess what, I say punjab. I swear, I think my parents  have probably begun to think I'm a little insane too. But, honestly, I don't know why I have such a big connection, with a land I've never even lived on for more than 6 months.

   I don't know if it's the smell of the early morning dew on the grass, the simplicity of the villagers, the familiar faces that resemble my forefathers, the hospitality of the villagers, or the "sadghi" of pind dihaan kuriyan. The trips to the pind each time leave me with a sensation of "apna pun", and every time it's time to leave, I cry, as if it's my doli!! ...

   I know I'll never be able to go back there, and make that house that I've always wanted to, as life is taking a new stride for me. But, I always do look back at my pind, and think, how can I make the lives of those who have made our lives possible (i.e. given my father and his family the love/blessings they have received from the pind) better? We've established a library in the school, and give out scholarships each year so that kids can afford to go to high educational institutes. But, for some reason, this always feels short.

 SSA Ji

question: marriage, death, 2 souls...how does it work?
answer:
> so what is the translation meant to be then?

In  the following verse :-

ਮਃ  ੩  ॥
Mėhlā 3.
Third Mehl:

ਧਨ ਪਿਰੁ ਏਹਿ ਨ ਆਖੀਅਨਿ ਬਹਨਿ ਇਕਠੇ ਹੋਇ ॥
Ḏẖan pir ehi na ākẖī▫an bahan ikṯẖe ho▫e.
They are not said to be husband and wife, who merely sit together.

ਏਕ ਜੋਤਿ ਦੁਇ ਮੂਰਤੀ ਧਨ ਪਿਰੁ ਕਹੀਐ ਸੋਇ ॥੩॥
Ėk joṯ ḏu▫e mūrṯī ḏẖan pir kahī▫ai so▫e. ||3||
They alone are called husband and wife, who have one light in two bodies. ||3||

 ਜੋਤਿ (  joṯ ) has many interpretations such as ( Light, soul,spiritual knoweldge(same as 'gyan') , Flame of light, luster, brilliance, fire, God. ,Holding)

In my view (though  i can be wrong) , here  ਜੋਤਿ (  joṯ ) means some kind of knoweldge, ( they share same understanding and comprehend each other ) . In punjabi language this word has more-like spirtual meaning but It is also oftenly used as a substitute of Divine knoweldge (  Gyan  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyan_(sanskrit)   , Bharam gyan etc. )

question: Visiting Punjab - need travel advice
answer:
[member] Ji ---

I cannot offer specific information about serais, perhaps someone else will chime in. However, here are few general ideas that I learned while traveling in India for six weeks in 2005:

1. Airport is the best place to perfom money exchanges (difficult in Punjab).
2. Wear a money belt or a fishernan's jacket under your shirt with mulitple pocket to keep your money and important papers.
3. Keep enough money in convenient pocket to pay as you go (do no let anybody know that you are carrying a lot of rupees).
4. Avoid particpating in drinking parties if you can (even with your former friends!).
5. You are taking a big risk if you do not stay in safe and secure (high end) places.
6. Try to dress like the locals so that they do not recognize that you came from a foreign land. This is hard to do.
7. Keep all your papers and money in plastic zippers so that they do not get wet for whatever reason.
8. I drank only bottled water, careful with food as well. I enjoyed Dhaba food!
9. It is quite easy to hire a car (in Punjab).

This is all I can offer. By the way I visited Kolkata, Bangalore, Mysore, Delhi, and Amritsar without any serious problem over a period of six weeks in 2005. Have a happy trip!

question: Visiting Punjab - need travel advice
answer:
Takhat Damdama Saheb at Sabo ki Talwandi some 30 kilometers from Bhatinda has a large newly constructed rest house for visiting sangat ( we saw it on our visit but did not choose to stay there as we had booking in Bhatinda).
If the day you visit does not have some samagam or congregation of Akali party there, you should be able to get a room to sleep over.
Bhatinda has several hotels. At least one of them is patronized by the executives of various companies(power plant, refinery under construction etc.) who have business there is fairly good. Only make sure you do not land up on some festival or public holiday as hotel service is not available on such days (surprise!). We had booked rooms there but on the arrival, which was Diwali day, the hotel told us that no service was available as all staff was on holiday. The same stroy was repeated at all smaller hotels as well in Bhatinda. However, we could find accomodation in one of the resort on the highway to Amritsar.
We travelled in car from Delhi and were at the Takhat by lunch time and did join the langar there.
Have a nice trip.

Guru fateh.

question: Guru Nanak's actual birth date?
answer:
None of the above! Reason being that the birth date of Guru Nanak is calculated using Bikrami calendar (traditional calendar used in India) and falls on Pooranmasi (full moon) of kattak or Vaisakh depending upon whom do you believe!

Traditional view used Guru Nanak's birth date as pooranmasi of kattak in 1469 citing old janamsakhi of Bhai Bala and some other texts. Karam Singh first challenged that date and stated that it was not kattak but Vaisakh of 1469 when Guru Nanak was born. He wrote detailed explanation on his findings in his work called "Kattak ke Visakh". Most modern historians and scholars have accepted his work and also agree with him that Guru Nanak was born on Visakhi of 1469. The date would be March 27th, 1469. It was not a mere co-incidence that Visakhi of 1699 was used again by 10th Guru Sahib for the initiation of Khalsa.

This leads to the next obvious question that if we now know and have it confirmed that Guru Nanak was born on poornamasi of Vaisakh, then why not use that date? The problem is some groups in India refuse to change the dates from traditional Hindu calendar and therefore Guru Nanak's birthday is still shown in Sep. month along with some other historical dates. Also, another thing to consider is, should we choose Mar. 27th as Guru Nanak's date or pooranmasi of Visakh?

A lot has been written on this and unfortunately, Sikhs have not agreed upon the date yet!

question: getting initiated into skihism
answer:
> I had first come across sikhism 8 months back, at that time when I heard the word ekonkar something touched me deeply within. it was like a Light. I have been reading the Hukamnama daily ever since but would  like to know how it is used in prayers, how it is meant to be read & basically want to learn the methods of praying etc.
> i have been trying to do as much online research as I can but couldnt find much on how exactly the Hukamnama is meant to be prayed. would appreciate any help.

Gurfateh,

 THere is indeed a specific method with which the Hukamnama is read,

 I will provide here all the details as per the guidelines of Sikhpride.com

Skip to step 6 if you are reciting from an online source

> Here's a step by step way of taking the hukamnama:
>
> 1. An Ardaas or standing prayer, should be offered before taking a Hukamnama.
>
> 2. If Guru Ji is covered with a Rumaala Sahib (beautiful fabric draping), then slowly
> with reverence roll or fold the Rumaala Sahib on itself. It is advisable to tuck the
> rolled up section of the Rumaala Sahib between the hard cover of Sri Guru Granth
> Sahib and the Angs on both sides. Ang litterally means 'part' as in part of a body. Each
> ang is reverently considered to be part of the body of the living Guru, Sri Guru Granth
> Sahib ji.
>
> 3. If Guru Ji has not been opened, then when opening Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the
> opening angs at the top will be the Hukamnama. If Guru is already open then from the
> middle of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, lift an equal amount of Angs from one side and
> the other side, and with both thumbs carefully and randomly select an ang from the
> middle section of Guru Ji.
>
> 4. Before reciting a Hukamnama, it is common to recite a mangla-chaaran, which means
> an invocation. We not only invoke the blessing of the Guru but clear our minds that
> we may read the Hukamnaama with proper attention. This can be a small shabad,
> salokh or saying 'Satnaam Vaahiguroo' in between opening Guru Ji for the
> Hukamnama and before reading the Hukam.
>
> Some examples of Mangla-chaarans which are commonly used when taking
> Hukamnamas are:
> - 1. Mool Mantar: -
> "One Universal Creator God. The Name Is Truth. Creative Being Personified. No
> Fear. No Hatred. Image Of The Undying, Beyond Birth, Self-Existent. By Guru's
> Grace." (Ang 1, SGGS)
>
> 2. Salokh (couplet):
> "Salokh: I bow down, and fall to the ground in humble adoration, countless times, to
> the All-powerful Lord, who possesses all powers. Please protect me, and save me
> from wandering, God. Reach out and give Nanak Your Hand. ||1||" (Ang 256, SGGS)
>
> 3. A pauree (stanza) from a shabad:
> "I seek Your Sanctuary - You are my only hope. You are my companion, and my best
> friend. Save me, O Merciful Saviour Lord; Nanak is the slave of Your home. ||3||12||"
> (Ang 673)
>
>
> 5. The Hukamnama according to the Rehat Maryada is always from the top left hand
> side. If the shabad is continuing from the previous ang turn the ang over to the point
> where the shabad begins.
>
> If the Bani is a Salokh (couplet) or a Pauree (stanza), read the Salokh and the Pauree
> (if it starts on the previous ang, start from there). The pauree typically at the end of a
> given Shabad, which is deliniated by the pause or 'Rahao' line, in a shabad contains
> the central idea of Guru Ji's message. The other stanzas then expound in greater detail
> on this central theme.
>
> 6. You need to read the first two lines of the Hukamnama twice. Again the Pauree
> before the "Rahaao" (if applicable) is usually the central idea of the Shabad. The last
> two lines are then to also read twice (as indication that this is the end of the
> Hukamnama).
>
> 7. A shabad usually ends with "Nanak" Also you can tell by looking at the numbers
> following after the line after a given Pauree where you are. The final Pauree contains
> a number then another number indicating fianlity of the Shabad. Thus Gurbani is
> organized in a logical way most can follow.

question: The Hypocrisy of Knowledge
answer:
Ek OnKaar Sat Naam

[member] ji,

This was an interesting thought-provoking article.Thank you for the link.

It is anybody's guess as to how mankind will evolve, or even how other species will evolve.
When greed takes hold, and the ball starts rolling, with no counter-balancing force, anything can happen (as mentioned in the article with repect to regard for native Americans).

We do not know how  increased knowledge will affect mankind, but from past history and current state of people in the least developed nations we know for certain that not all people will benefit, and many will actually suffer greatly as a result of the deprivation of access to resources in their own native countries, whilst those with knowledge, capital and technology will exploit them to the full. People get shited out from localities they have lived in for generations, at the drop of a hat. If they show resistance, then we may not even hear from them again.

There are many potential hazards with new technology, increasing use of resources and burgeoning populations.

eg computers are being developed with bacteria:

[link]
Is there a real risk  such computers will  begin to take over at some point in time, if they are allowed to "evolve"?

Then there are risks of geneticaly modified foods, which are now used ad-hoc in some countries.
Any defects may lead to irreversible adverse long-term effects, but the people making money now from GM foods and seeds will be long-gone.

Then there is possible huge changes in climate, as use of fossil fuels continues to increase with no end in sight, despite all the debates for more green approches. Rising sea-levels will wipe out many islands, and low-lying areas, such as big parts of Bangladesh - where will these people go? Salt will affect inland rivers and water tables, such as in Punjab - previously the bread basket of India/Pakistan - they will have to resort to seeds like GM rice etc that can grow in salt water.

The interminable rise in populations, especially where religion determines whether birth control methods are used or not used, will put strain on local resources, and lead to conflicts, over food, water and resources. In a quest for survival, people will naturally seek to emigrate, if at all possible. Will countries accept them out of humanitarian compassion, or will higher and higher border fences be put up?

The increased populations also make it easier for diseases to spread. New diseases can also wipe out populations very quickly ( eg when europeans went to central and south americas). The effect of diseases cannot be underestimated, and with biological weapons also in abundance, it only takes some irresponsible behaviour to lead to opening of the Pandora's box.

Man's greed is insatiable, and may be its complete undoing. Knowledge can be used in vain attempts to self-satisfy, which in the long term are doomed to fail future generations, or can be used in compassion for others.

Sat Sri Akal

question: yogi bhajan singh ji an ordinary human being?
answer:
No offence to the memory of Yogi Harbhajan Singh Jee but I would narrate one prsonal experience I had with him.He certainly did quite some pioneering work in spreading Skhi in America and was a sucessful enterpreneur. He set up a community which is active and thriving.

It was about the last quarter of 1972 and I was in the postgraduate program at [place]. The room was full of American Sikhs, every body sat on carpets and Yogi was before a podium. I was probably only Sikh of Indian origin in the audience. There was a question/ answer session after his talk and I did ask him a question about place of yoga in Sikhism and his reply was that Guru Nanak's son was one of the greatest Yogi. I knew that his son and his son was not part of the sikhi I knew, so I left it at that.

question: Beginning to research Sikhism, questions...
answer:
Dear [member],

Wecome to Sikhism. This is a good site to start with. Look for Sikh Resources on the site, which in brief explains principles, belief and practices of sikhism. Then, there is Sikh Rehat Maryada (Sikh Code of Conduct) also available on this site which describes who is Sikh and what she/he is expected to do to follow the Sikh religion.

The topic of hair is also covered in the above mentioned documents. In brief, one is not expected to remove, shape, cut body hair irrespective of gender. Dreadlock is not the norm as one is expected to keep the head hair combed and cleaned.

You can also search for discussion on most of the subject of Sikh interest on this discussion forum to start with and progress to weblinks on Sikhiwiki for various publications and books. Singh Brothers in Amritsar, India, are one of the major publishers and suppliers of books on Sikhism.

I hope others will fill you up with much more information on the subject, if you visit/ stay on this forum.

Wahe Guru Ji Ka Khalsa, Wahe Guru Ji Ki Fateh

question: Interreligious marriage for Gursikh allowed?
answer:
It is my experience that most Sikh Indian girls in the West at least flirt with the idea of marrying outside the faith for various reasons. Perhaps they think that Sikh Indian men cannot be fashionable enough for them.

That said, setting aside all rules and rehats, the basic definition of marriage in Sikhism implies a union of two souls into one soul that resides in two bodies. Is that possible with a non-Sikh ? I cannot say no in all cases (as there are many religious traditions that work more or less harmoniously with Sikhi), but given the views of Sikhism (and other non - my-way-or-the-highway religions) prevalent in proselytizing religions like Christianity and Islam, seems extremely unlikely.

I also think that people have a right to make what choices they want, but should refrain from the hypocrisy in continuing to claim affiliation with a way of life they have turned their back on. The lady you reference (perhaps) and the current Methodist Republican Sarah Palin endorsed (the ideology represented by that combination should make any Sikh, or even any person with a basic understanding and respect for human dignity, cringe) Sikh-when-convenient candidate for Governor of South Carolina are just examples of people who persist in dragging the name of Sikhi through the mud-dle (pun intended) of their personal choices.

I have observed this in my extended family (I have a thread on this very topic) where Sikh tolerance is being used to hide/enable a multitude of behaviours that are grossly inconsistent with Sikhi. Sikhi, in my opinion, starts with self-respect (not haumae or ego). If you do not respect yourself enough to not keep any cordial contact with people who do not respect you, then everything else about you has to be seen as being either weak-willed or fake.

> The 2006 civil registration bill requires citizens to identify their religion on National Identity Cards (KTP). The bill does not allow citizens to identify themselves as anything outside of the six recognized religious groups. Legally, citizens may leave the religious section blank, but some local government officials were not familiar with this option. Members of unrecognized religious groups were often unable to obtain KTPs as a result.

How even in practice, the people filling them out don't know the procedure to list them as not a practicioner of one of the 6.

> The Ministry of Religious Affairs extends official status to six religious groups: Islam, Catholicism, Protestantism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Confucianism. Although these groups have the right to establish a house of worship, obtain identity cards, and register marriages and births, they face administrative difficulties in doing so. question: Why are Sikh Gurdwaras so loud?
answer: It is an ego issue with the priest and corruption that laws never get implemented. May be because a developing country goes through this phase. First of all there shouldnt be more than single gurudwara in a village and there are many based ON castes. I just hope that the SGPC committee takes note of this. This creates problem in meditation and PATH as said above

extra.question_body:
I don't mean to be disrespectful to the gurudwaras, however after living in Punjab for a while, I have often come across this problem. The gurudwaras almost throughout Punjab turn on their loudspeakers early in the morning. The noise level is usually over 100 decibels and can be heard from a distance. Sometimes there are two or three gurudwaras in the vicinity and when all of them turn on their loudspeakers, it's hard to figure out who's saying what.
They speak rapidly while repeating the shalokas. And are loud enough to disrupt a person's sleep or in my case, I find it really hard to meditate in the morning due to the noise.

Noise over 85 decibels can cause permanent hearing loss, so if somebody is close to the loudspeakers it can be harmful to their health.

I am quite confused about how exactly Sikhism is practised. My understanding is that it would make sense for an individual to read the holy book in the morning and not hear it from a loudspeaker. And an individual should have a choice to listen to somebody repeating what they are reading from the holy book and it shouldn't be forced on him or her.

I respect Sikhism, but I think that the use of loudspeakers should not be a part of Sikh religion. It is almost offensive in my opinion. How would a sikh like it if I was to read my favorite holy book (not from Sikh religion) loud into their ears?

According to the noise pollution laws in India, it is prohibited to make noise exceeding 55 decibels during the day and 45 decibels before 6 am. Yet the gurudwaras and even other temples seem to ignore this law.

It is my sincere request to all the Sikh governing organizations to respect other people's privacy and let them pursue their own religions by not using the loudspeakers.

And please don't take it as an offense. As I mentioned, I have respect for Sikhism and all other religions, but I just can't figure out why a religion should be forced on somebody.

What is your opinion about this issue? I'm quite curious about what Sikhs think about it? What can be done about it if you think that my views are right?

question: Why are Sikh Gurdwaras so loud?
answer:
[member],

As stated above, this isn't exclusive to Sikhism, this is cultural phenomenon which is applied in India by Sikhs, Hindu's and Muslims alike. Were you to be residing a an areas whose populace was predominately Hindu or Muslim, you would encounter the same, though the time of when it occurs might be different.

So the loudspeakers are not a part of Sikhism but more of culture. You will have no doubt noticed during your time in India, more often than not, the people find themselves associating themselves with ritual and culture more so than the effective practice of their religion.

However one of the primary reasons for having these loudspeakers (especially in villages) is that there is a high level of illiteracy in these villages, especially among the older generations and for some reading the holy scriptures is not an option and the next best thing is the ability to hear the prayers being recited. Prayers penetrating the ears is considered a blessing and the reason for the loudspeakers is to provide a service and not an attempt to force the religion on someone.

You could approach the local gurdwara with a polite request, however I am not sure how far that will get you but at least it is an attempt at direct dialogue.

question: Why are Sikh Gurdwaras so loud?
answer:
Waheguru Ji ka Khalsa Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh.....

I know it can be very problematic sometimes.... But in the past at the time of our Gurus, the Gurudwaras just to beat Nagaare (Huge Battle Drums) right at 2:30 am or so just to wake people up just in case they didn't get up by themselves....

Over the time the practice has declined and now this practice is being followed only at Harmandir Sahib.... All the other Gurudwaras use loud speakers instead to wake people up.... They do not deliberately intend to disturb someone in meditation....

I've been irritated for months by my neighbor next door who snores just too much Loud.... In winter when its too quite at 3:00 am in the morning it just to bother me so much in my meditation and I started using wet cotton to plug my ears to establish absolute silence.... Later when I progressed in my meditation, one day I didn't plug my ears and surprising nothing could disturb me anymore in my concentration.... By Guru's grace snoring started sounding rather sweet to me.....

So I really suggest that you don't give your attention to the loud speaker and rather appreciate that its Gurbani though it doesn't sound good.... As you harmonize within yourself through meditation nothing with bother you in your meditation anymore....

Regards....

question: New to the Sikh faith.... need guidance!
answer:
[member]-

You've made the first step and reached out on a public forum! Great! I would also suggest posting ads on local networks like craigslist or kijiji for your area, looking for English-speaking contacts at your local Gurudwara. Also see if local universities and colleges have Sikh student groups (I am making the assumption you are a young adult by your language, please correct me if I am wrong), as it is less intimidating connecting with youth your own age.

However, don't judge a book by its cover; my first two contacts in the Sikh community when I first stepped into it were older gentlemen whose first language was not English, but they spoke it very well and were very welcoming and friendly. Even just having one contact at the Gurudwara can make going a lot less stressful and awkward.

You may just have to take the plunge eventually and just go to the Gurudwara, but you can always look for tips on how to act and dress before going, and maybe take along an open-minded friend so that it's less intimidating. It can be a very nerve-wracking experience, but it's worth it if you know this is the path for you! Don't let anything deter you. I participated in this forum for quite some time before actually starting to attend the Gurudwara regularly.

Best of luck, hope this helped at least a little bit!

question: New member seeks advice
answer:
I am glad to hear that you want to learn about Sikhism.  Sikh means ‘student’, and learning is the core of Sikhism.  The Sikh scripture, Shri Guru Granth Sahib (SGGS), which is a compilation of hymns written by six of the ten Gurus, and 30 other godly souls who belonged to diverse walks of life and faiths.  SGGS, the living Guru of the Sikhs, tells us that a Sikh is a child of the Lord, and therefore all the God’s prophets and saints belong to the Sikhs.  Sikhs are urged to abandon faults, and build partnerships based on virtues with whomever we meet.

I grew up in a Sikh household and learnt Sikhism naturally by osmosis.  Therefore, I may not be the best person to refer you to resources for beginners.  Many others on this site, especially the ones who adopted Sikhism may be much better qualified.

Resources on Sikhism can be generally divided into the following three categories: Historical, Philosophical interpretations and Gurbani (Guru’s word or advice).  If you can manage to invest time, the best rewards are in Gurbani.  However, going directly to Gurbani may be a bit difficult for a beginner, and you may wish to work with all three.   The following is a brief description of each:

Historical:  Let me start by saying, that even though all of the ten Gurus were prolific writers and patrons of scholarship, they went out of their way to avoid leaving behind any biographies or paintings of themselves.   In my view, this was done for two reasons: 1) Gurus wanted Sikhs to worship and focus only on God and nothing but God, and didn’t want to create a hero cult which often forms around prophets. 2) Physical (rituals) and familiar (worldly stories), is where the human comfort zone lies, and given even half a chance, we quickly latch on to the physical.  Gurus instead wanted Sikhs to concentrate on ‘word’ for building a bond with God who is beyond any physical characteristics.   It may be OK, for a beginner, to rely on the historical literature to understand the context and to draw some inspiration to get started, but it’s best if your main guidance comes from Gurbani.   Unfortunately, the historical literature is also rife with authors focusing excessively on miracles and the supernatural in an effort to aggrandize their chosen faith.   In the category of historical literature, Sikh History by Max McAuliffe is a good source.  Online, you can also find good materials on SikhiWiki.

Philosophical Interpretation: There is a lot of literature online in this category.  You may want to start by searching something as simple as ‘100 Questions about Sikhism’, and then drill into areas which interest you.  Once again, as in any interpretation, you have to be mindful of the biases of the author.  When we touch a flower, we transfer fragrance from the flower to our hands, in the same process, we transfer our body oil and smell from our hands to the flower.  Once a flower has been touched by many hands, it starts to smell more like hands than a flower.  When reading these interpretations, it’s important to validate them against Gurbani, the unadulterated fragrance.

Gurbani:  There are very good translations of SGGS online.  Many people relate easily to Sukhmani Sahib (192 hymns starting on page 262 of SGGS).

Progress is made by living what one learns.  It’s not necessary to read a lot of Gurbani; read however much you are comfortable with.  It’s good to create a routine, contemplate and then practice what you read.  God is everywhere and in everybody.  It’s important to be thankful for what we have, and to love everybody.   Any sort of discrimination takes us away from God.  If we cannot see God in all, we cannot see God at all.

Regards

question: similar jat gotra marriage question
answer:
[member],

Most of the Jatt families, belonging to Sikh religion, shy away from marrying among own and mother's gotra.  Some, less commonly, will also include grandmothers' maiden gotras on the no-marriage list.  These rules were probably put in place, long time ago, to avoid inter-breeding and to reduce friction in the rural community structure.  These days many move out of their ancestral villages, and population size in most gotras are huge (thus diluting the inter-breeding argument).  As a result, these days, breaking gotra rules are not uncommon.

Things are different among Jatt families in Muslim and Hindu religions.  Muslims have no gotra qualms and often marry their cousins.  Hindu Jatts, especially in rural Haryana, are brutally against people who marry among off-limit gotras; Vitriol from gotra panchayats in Haryana have led to assaults and murders of those who step outside the gotra boundaries.

The objection and its intensity will depend upon your families and where you live.  One of my friends in Canada, a Gill married another Gill with blessing from both families.  About fifty years ago, there was a case in my ancestral village where some families boycotted a family for marrying their daughter out of gotra bounds.  Few in my village took this boycott seriously, and it fizzled out very quickly.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

There is nothing wrong in celebrating with your family, friends and neighbours.

This festival of Holi is assosiated with the devotion of Bhagat Prahlad. So, we can learn a lot from Bhagat Prahlad.

ਪ੍ਰਹਲਾਦ ਪਠਾਏ ਪੜਨ ਸਾਲ॥

question: bani  kanth
answer:
Keep at it, it comes naturally.  Even if it doesn't, its nothing to be embarrassed about.  The purpose of gurbani is to understand it and then live it; not merely memorize it.  Our forefathers chose their words carefully, and called it "paath karna"(i.e. do or live gurbani) not  "paath parhna" (i.e. read gurbani).  Reading or listening is the first important step in understanding Guru's instructions.  Daily reading is necessary, because our mind gets incessant feed of temptations, and daily reminder of Guru's instructions is an antidote.

When properly understood and followed, even a single of verse of gurbani is enough to change a person's life.  There is a famous anecdote from Guru Gobind Singh ji's time.  Guru ji placed a lot of emphasis on education, and had organized lessons for Sikhs in Anandpur Sahib.  One day, Guru ji summoned a volunteer to teach gurbani to an illiterate but otherwise a very devout Sikh.  The Sikh didn't show after the first lesson of gurbani.  The volunteer went to Guruji, and complained about Sikh's tardiness.  Guru ji sent for the Sikh and asked him to explain, why he never showed after the first lesson.  The Sikh said, that on the first day, he was taught "Anand peya meri maye, Satguru mein paya".  He said, since then he has been reciting the verse and has been in anand (bliss), and didn't feel the need for anything else.

So my suggestions:
1) Don't feel bad about not being able to memorize gurbani.  2) Set a target on how much gurbani you wish to read everyday, and then stick to it (if you can keep up with the 5 banis in our prescribed maryada, its wonderful!).  3) If you have difficulty understanding, set a target for yourself to understand the meaning of so many new verses everyday.  4) Finally, pick one verse, whose meaning you understand, and then reflect on it all day, and try to live it as much as possible.

question: Lack of scholars and divisions
answer:
Here are a few causes:
People serving in the gurdwara often lack spiritual insight or college education.
As a result, speakers with questionable motives are allowed to occupy our time.
The service is structured so that the sangat is held hostage by a speaker or singer.
Gurdwaras are now used for collecting money, for personal fame and for politics.
Almost anyone can stand up and interfere in a gurdwara.

Possible solutions:

Select only spiritually motivated and educated individuals to serve in a gurdwara.

Election of like-minded members by the ignorant majority is not suitable for managing the gurdwaras.
See related topic: [link]

Gurdwara services need modification so that people can feel free to walk-out, have tea or have langar to occupy their time when they do not approve a speaker or a singer.

Gurdwaras cannot improve as long as we sell parshad, paath, and other services.

The archaic custom of ‘throwing’ money in front of the Guru creates havoc. Pay with a check, credit card, or get a receipt for cash, not just drop money in a box.

Negativity, discussing politics literature etc. should not be allowed in the presence of Guru Granth Sahib. Such items should be discussed outside.

In the modern times, there is no need to associate our gurdwara with politics. Our political issues need to be tackled from outside the gurdwaras.

We have become accustomed to using the gurdwara for quasi-religious cultural and social events. We need to learn to attend and pay for such events outside the gurdwara.

If we reserved the gurdwara for pure gurbani we will change the kind of people who swarm the gurdwaras.

Difference of opinions and views is healthy and in fact shows that Sikh community is still actively seeking! Even other communities go through it and have various sections. Some are much worse than Sikhs; Shiaas and Sunnis in Islam, who literally bomb each other, various factions under Christianity and even Buddhism.

These days we have a small minority of factional groups of Sikhs, who are always trying to hijack every difference of opinion. For these groups, everything is about AKJ, Damdami Taksal or Missionary Sikhs and they can seldom support each other. Vast majority of Sikhs who neither associate or care about these factions just want to go to Gurudwara and listen to kirtan or discourse and participate for what little time they have.

It is up to the Sikh community to figure how to handle these factions or their complaints. Unfortunately, Jathedars of Sikh panth have failed miserably in giving a decent direction in such instances. We had Sikh scholars in the past who had different opinions but they were well respected by everyone. Prof. Sahib Singh, Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, Sant Singh ji Maskeen etc. were all well respected Sikh scholars and the key to their success was that they did not indulge in needless controversies all the time. They had their differences but they also realized that there are bigger and important issues on hand. Bhai Kahn Singh Ji Nabha had clear stance on Ragmala when this controversy was creating a lot of rift between the Sikh community, but he also insisted that Sikhs need to move on and focus on future.

Same should be done today. All of us can't agree on same views and interpretations and that's fine. There are some fundamentals to Sikhism which need to be adhered to but at the same time, we have to leave room for other customs, traditions and changes which will continue to happen. Sikh community will go through changes just like everything else but they need to keep their fundamentals strong and allow diverse views and opinions on other aspects.

question: A Question about Hair
answer:
Waheguru ji ka Khalsa.  Waheguru ji ki Fateh.

Greetings ji.  Remember that each hair naturally falls out every 3 years or so (for most people), so if you take good care of your hair and cover it, either with a dastaar or a scarf of some kind, it should stay healthy.  Keeping the hair open to the elements 24/7 is the major thing that causes split ends.  Also, when you brush it, start from the ends and work your way to the root, don’t pull it!  Only brush your hair when it is dry.  Pulling the hair with a comb or brush, especially when it is wet, causes it to stretch and causes split ends as well.  Be patient if you get a knot and comb it gently.   If your hair feels dry and crunchy, rub a little organic coconut oil into the ends and work that to the root.  Don’t use too much or it will just feel gross and oily.  And don’t use shampoo every day.  Shampoo is very drying too.  If you shower every day, only actually wash your hair every other or ever two days (unless you have a health issue that causes you to need to wash it every day).  Hope this helps!

extra.question_body:
Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh,

Sikhi places great emphasis on the notion that all human beings are of equal intrinsic value. Yet a great many of my Sikh brothers and sisters here in the United Kingdom, perhaps due to nostalgia for the good old days of the Empire in which the Sikhs were highly regarded and fought loyally for the Crown, are thorough royalists. I however have always been of the opinion that Sikhi is inextricably opposed to the idea of a monarchy. Guru Gobind Singh Ji's innovation of investing the entire Panth with authority [i.e. the Panth would rule itself and reach decisions at gatherings known as Sarbat Khalsa] was, it seems to me, one of the forerunners of republicanism, a proto-democracy. This is one of the reasons Maharaja Ranjit Singh committed a grave misdeed in establishing himself as King of all Sikhs.

The lavish lifestyle of the British Royal Family, is funded from the pocket of taxpayers, myself among them, whether we agree with the monarchical institution or not. The royals do not work to earn their obscene wealth. They do not share this money with the less fortunate.

No freedom of choice. No hard work. No dissemination of wealth. Aren't these values, which are disdained by the royals, not some of the cornerstones of the Sikh faith, and indeed, many other faiths?

question: Obsession and Sikhism
answer:
There is nothing wrong in praying to God for being with somebody.  Sikhs have to avoid things which make us forget God.  If the urge to be with somebody is making you talk to God, you are a lucky man.  Whatever the outcome, if you can find it in yourself to thank god, you will be luckier still.  Sikhism is a fun ride full of love and joy, it's not an austere dry path.  With the exception of harming somebody, we should ask from God whatever we desire.  You can draw inspiration from Bhagat Dhanna ji's negotiations for a good wife and other worldly things in exchange for worshipping God (SGGS 695):

ਗੋਪਾਲ ਤੇਰਾ ਆਰਤਾ ॥
O Lord of the world, this is Your lamp-lit worship service.

ਜੋ ਜਨ ਤੁਮਰੀ ਭਗਤਿ ਕਰੰਤੇ ਤਿਨ ਕੇ ਕਾਜ ਸਵਾਰਤਾ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ ॥
You are the Arranger of the affairs of those humble beings who perform Your devotional worship service. ||1||Pause||

ਦਾਲਿ ਸੀਧਾ ਮਾਗਉ ਘੀਉ ॥
Lentils, flour and ghee - these things, I ask of You.

ਹਮਰਾ ਖੁਸੀ ਕਰੈ ਨਿਤ ਜੀਉ ॥
My mind shall ever be pleased.

ਪਨ੍ਹ੍ਹੀਆ ਛਾਦਨੁ ਨੀਕਾ ॥ ਅਨਾਜੁ ਮਗਉ ਸਤ ਸੀ ਕਾ ॥੧॥
Shoes, fine clothes, and grain of seven kinds - I ask of You.

ਗਊ ਭੈਸ ਮਗਉ ਲਾਵੇਰੀ ॥
A milk cow, and a water buffalo, I ask of You,

ਇਕ ਤਾਜਨਿ ਤੁਰੀ ਚੰਗੇਰੀ ॥
and a fine Turkestani horse.

ਘਰ ਕੀ ਗੀਹਨਿ ਚੰਗੀ ॥ ਜਨੁ ਧੰਨਾ ਲੇਵੈ ਮੰਗੀ ॥੨॥੪॥
A good wife to care for my home -  Your humble servant Dhanna asks for these things, Lord. ||2||4||

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh

question: Gurbani as a guide?
answer:
In my rather simplistic understanding, Gurbani is not like doctor's prescrition that say take one three times a day for one week and finish the course.  Neither it is like the times tables one learns in rota fashion at very early age.   It cannot be spoon fed either. There are no procedures and processes in it like the army manuals which tell you how you are supposed to do everything from getting up in the morning to going to bed at night.   Soldiers trained trained are not able to deal with even slightly unfamiliar situations. This is why military has so called elite divisions, whose soldiers are more flexible.

Gurbani has to be read line by line and then understood not just in terms of words but also of actions.  If you get stuck on some line because you don't understand the words or how to interpret it in the context then you need to find someone to explain. How do you know the person has the understanding?  This is why conferring with sadh sangat it suggested by Gurbani.

Once you understand it then you are able to work out for yourself what to do in every situation you face in this life.

question: Potential convert nervous about going to Gurdwara
answer:
[member],

Welcome to the forum, I hope you gain valuable insight into Sikhism.

why don't you let us know where you live and if there are any Sikhs on this forum who live nearby maybe they could take you along to your Gurdwara.

Otherwise I would encourage to you pluck up courage and go along to your local Gurdwara. Either go on a Saturday afternoon, normally it will be quiet, as a weekly service takes place on Sunday mornings, there  are often some program going on, on a Saturday evening, else go on a Sunday morning when you will meet a lot more Sikhs. Take a covering for your head, a scarf if you are a lady or a large handkerchief if you are a bloke.

I would suggest you approach a young person, they are more open and liberal minded. Some older people can be quite abrasive and cantankerous and I wouldn't take this personally they are like this with most people, especially the young. Approach a young person and explain that it is your first time at the Gurdwara and you would like a little assistance, I am sure they will welcome you and show you around. In time you will meet young people and build a good relationship.

All the best.

question: Turban Day - Good or Bad Idea, your thoughts?
answer:
Waheguru ji ka khalsa
Waheguru ji ki fateh

There are two sides of every coin.

Before making any decision, one must look at the Positive side and ensure that Good outweighs bad aspect.

I think Turban Day is a good idea.

It creates awareness and demonstrates that Sikhs are friendly people.

What you need is big sponsors to fund this Seva.

Normally Daya or compassion is a characteristic of Khatri's - highest class.

Now don't confuse being Khatri with caste or surname.

Khatri means Ruling or Warrior class, so unless someone belongs to present day political or dictator family, the term has no meaning.

In order to fund Big community service projects you need support from Rich & Powerful people.

Rather than stopping such projects plan on getting wealthy Patrons.

You can also collaborate with local Gurdwaras to partly fund such initiatives.

Waheguru ji ka khalsa
Waheguru ji ki fateh

P.S - Keep up the good work

extra.question_body:
Waheguru Jio,

*disclaimer: I do happen to operate an online store that sells turbans and we donate a lot of Turbans, to seniors, folks with financial difficulty (most of the request there get screened) and to Sikh camps.

I have been tying a Turban/Dastaar everyday since 1998-1999.  So, everyday is Turban Day.   I am not a big fan of making Turban a Hallmark Day that people remember once a year.   I also happen to not be a fan of us putting on Turbans on passerbys who we solicit to see if they want to wear a Turban.  Then we take a picture of them wearing a Turban and we then market that all over Facebook and other social media sites.

My Turban and by association, all Turbans are sacred.  It is not a photo opportunity.  It is not like a Japanese Kimono or a Cowboy outfit that one wears to take a photo.   This has been going on for a few years and more and more campus teams are writing to us asking for Turban cloth material.

I want to support Turban wearing Sikhs, I want to support those Sikhs that want to wear a Turban and are considering wearing one regularly.  I want to support Sikhs who are considering growing their Kesh.  I want to support anyone that respects the Turban for not only religious but the cultural value it has to our community.

So,  my position is:  Turban Day is a good idea as long as we are demonstrating turban tying on Sikhs, teaching our your Sikhs to tie a Turban.   Turban Day is a bad idea when we let anyone wear a Turban, even for 5 mins and a photo.

Your thoughts please.

question: ਿਵਸਰਗ or ਿਵਸਰ੍ਗ
answer:
Bhai [member],

I have only seen Visarg spelled as "ਵਿਸਰਗ".

Adding an "a" at the end is an Anglicized pronunciation of Sanskrit words.  This practice has always puzzled me because native speakers in India (of Punjabi, Hindi or Sanskrit) never say "Arjuna", "Ashoka", "Akasha" or "Yoga".  In India, these words are pronounced as  "Arjun", "Ashok", "Akash" or "Yog".   However, I am speaking as a lay man.  Unless a scholar of grammer can shed some light on this extra "a" at the end, my vote is to pronounce this word as "Visarg" and not "Visarga".

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh

answer:
First you need to ask yourself why you want to be a Sikh.

Is it for Spiritual or Temporal reasons.

Once you have a clarity of thought then start taking baby steps, don't rush.

If you can't travel daily then visit Gurdwara on weekends.

Start with one, either Kirtan or Punjabi classes.

I choose to visit a Gurdwara which is at 40 minutes drive rather then one which is 5.

Reason, it's open 24/7, excellant Kirtani's & Giani's, can always find Seva or listen to Akhand Paath.

So it all depends on whether you are willing enough !

question: Meaning of this shabad
answer:
[member] ji,

Ego is the strongest of the five evils, as it is at the root of the other four evils.  It’s the bane of human existence.  Ego hurts us in various ways:
•	Keeps us away from Naam/God.
•	Our pride is hurt very easily with real/imagined slights from others.  If we are not in a position to hit back at our perceived enemy, we stew inside and make ourselves miserable.  The Guru has likened ego to a thorn in our foot, it hurts us at every step.
•	In the cases, where we hold power/influence over others, ego drives us to do all sorts of cruel and unfair things to our fellow beings.

Ego works on us in stealth.   The Guru gave us the shabad below to liberate us from the misery of ego by challenging us to think about what ego really is.

ਮਾਰੂ ਮਹਲਾ ੫ ॥
Mārū mėhlā 5.

ਕਵਨ ਥਾਨ ਧੀਰਿਓ ਹੈ ਨਾਮਾ ਕਵਨ ਬਸਤੁ ਅਹੰਕਾਰਾ ॥
In what place does your false prestige (your name) reside? Where does egotism dwell?
Meaning:  Prestige and ego are not real things.  We think they are real only when we are asleep in maya.  Once we are self-aware, they disappear.
ਕਵਨ ਚਿਹਨ ਸੁਨਿ ਊਪਰਿ ਛੋਹਿਓ ਮੁਖ ਤੇ ਸੁਨਿ ਕਰਿ ਗਾਰਾ ॥੧॥
What injury have you suffered, listening to abuse from someone else's mouth? ||1||
Meaning: Be tolerant, and stop worrying about perceived or real slights.  Even when somebody curses you, it has no lasting effect on you.  Can you show me any scars on your face which were caused by somebody calling you names?
ਸੁਨਹੁ ਰੇ ਤੂ ਕਉਨੁ ਕਹਾ ਤੇ ਆਇਓ ॥
Listen: who are you, and where did you come from?
Meaning: Think about your real existence, and stop getting distracted by Maya.
ਏਤੀ ਨ ਜਾਨਉ ਕੇਤੀਕ ਮੁਦਤਿ ਚਲਤੇ ਖਬਰਿ ਨ ਪਾਇਓ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ ॥
You don't even know how long you will stay here; you have no hint of when you shall leave. ||1||Pause||
Meaning: Always be aware of your mortality and temporary existence.  Once somebody faces their mortality, their conduct automatically improves.  Once on death row, even hardened criminals repent and start introspection.
ਸਹਨ ਸੀਲ ਪਵਨ ਅਰੁ ਪਾਣੀ ਬਸੁਧਾ ਖਿਮਾ ਨਿਭਰਾਤੇ ॥
Wind and water have patience and tolerance; the earth has compassion and forgiveness, no doubt.
ਪੰਚ ਤਤ ਮਿਲਿ ਭਇਓ ਸੰਜੋਗਾ ਇਨ ਮਹਿ ਕਵਨ ਦੁਰਾਤੇ ॥੨॥
The union of the five tattvas - the five elements - has brought you into being. Which of these is evil? ||2||
Meaning: Our body is made up of five elements.  Wind, water and earth, the natural elements out of which we are built are known for their humility, tolerance and compassion.  Then where is our ego (evil) sprouting from?
ਜਿਨਿ ਰਚਿ ਰਚਿਆ ਪੁਰਖਿ ਬਿਧਾਤੈ ਨਾਲੇ ਹਉਮੈ ਪਾਈ ॥
The Primal Lord, the Architect of Destiny, formed your form; He also burdened you with egotism.
Meaning: Ego has been created by God himself.  Without ego his play of creation cannot work.
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣੁ ਉਸ ਹੀ ਕਉ ਹੈ ਰੇ ਓਹਾ ਆਵੈ ਜਾਈ ॥੩॥
He alone is born and dies; He alone comes and goes. ||3||
Meaning:  Realize this, it’s ego which is going through birth and death.  Its ego alone which is coming and going through cycles of life.
ਬਰਨੁ ਚਿਹਨੁ ਨਾਹੀ ਕਿਛੁ ਰਚਨਾ ਮਿਥਿਆ ਸਗਲ ਪਸਾਰਾ ॥
Nothing of the color and the form of the creation shall remain; the entire expanse is transitory.
Meaning: The whole thing is an illusion created by God.  Once he wraps up this illusion, no trace of this creation will remain.
ਭਣਤਿ ਨਾਨਕੁ ਜਬ ਖੇਲੁ ਉਝਾਰੈ ਤਬ ਏਕੈ ਏਕੰਕਾਰਾ ॥੪॥੪॥
Prays Nanak, when He brings His play to its close, then only the One, the One Lord remains. ||4||4||
Meaning: Once his world play is wrapped up then only one formless Lord shall remain.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

In other asthaans there have been incidents and special blessings or the Gurus have given their bachan at various asthaans that come true. This is the blessing of the Gurus so rejoice in this.

Go to any Gurdwara saroop of Guru Ji is their do darshan and do ardass to your Guru and He always listens, but remember “apay bij apay-he khow” – You reap what you sow.

question: Sikh Identity
answer: its a long history that eventually resulted in a saint soldier identity. During Guru Hargobind jis tie, Mughals passed an order that no one other than a muslim can wear a turban, ride a horse or keep a sword. a person can wear a small piece of cloth aroud his head to protect from cold and heat but not a turban. At this Guru Sahib sent messages across that his sikh will not see him unless he wears a turban of atleast 5 GAJ cloth, ride a horse and carry a sword. It was a revolutionary concept of equality, selfrespect and pride. Then in previous yugs whenever there was a problem or atrocities on bhagats, god always sent Bhagwan Ram, Bhagwan Krishna or any other avtars to sort out things by killing sinners like Ravan, Kans, etc. and maintained order on MAAT LOK. But in Kalyug, there are so many kans roaming around that God didn't just asked us to be a saint but a soldier as well to protect himself/ herself but also those who need help. a Sikhs life is just bhagti and sacrifice.

question: UK Caste Discrimination Legislation
answer:
SSA,

Laws and constitutional rights don't drive change, the change should be driven by the society at large, Laws and constitutional rights merely make it easier for society to adopt the changes.

Caste equality should be driven by society which means the traditionally higher caste should avoid falling in the trap of thinking and acting higher or better than others because of their caste. similarly on the other hand traditionally disadvantaged caste should stop accepting any form of affirmative advantage if their upbringing hasn't been disadvantaged due to their caste. e.g. had equal opportunity to education, school ,parent have equal opportunity in jobs and had equal opportunity in education.

So the law is not really going to make any difference, apart from ensuring cases of open caste discrimination are dealt with case by case.

question: paath
answer:
[member],

When Guruduara Act was formed in 1925, there were a lot of different practices in Sikhism.  SGPC set out to create Sikh Rehat Maryada to standardize these practices.  As part of this effort standard gutka of nitnem was also compiled.  Rehras in the SGPC gutka ends at Salok mehalaa 5|"Thaeraa keethaa jaatho naahee.  The SGPC maryada is most widely accepted but there are still some Sikh organizations (e.g. Damdami Taksal, Nanaksar, etc.) who have kept their own maryadas.  Damdami Taksal, for example prints a nitnem gutka which is called Sunder Gutka.  The Sunder Gutka has the longest version of Rehras which includes more shabads as well as excerpts from Dasam Granth.  Sri Harmandir Sahib is managed by SGPC and therefore follows the standard gutka.

Some people make these differences in maryada a point of contention.  Please follow whichever gutka you are comfortable with; its all gurbani.  The important thing is to contemplate and follow gurbani.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Sewa - are some types more blessed than others?
answer:
[member],

Sewa is selfless service, from the doer's perspective its sewa if its selfless , For the receiver perspective its importance is linked to how much is that particular sewa needed.

An deed done with thought\belief that its already blessed is not Sewa, its just an act or deed and is not selfless, The act\deed should be "kabool\Manjur" in the court of lord, only then is it considered blessed.

As to why most Sikhs generally indulge in the deed of providing food is partly due to langar (food) being an integral part of Sikh way of life and also coz is one of the very basic human necessity and one doesn't have to be broke or homeless to appreciate a good cooked meal.

As to which deed is most likely to be blessed in the court of lord ? No one really knows, so best is to do a deed that you are able to do and which is most needed by folks around you  (teach maths, give food, clothing etc ) and leave the blessing aspect on to later.

question: Re do lavaan
answer:
[member],

The objective of Sikhism is to do lavan.  By all means, please try and do lavan and may Guru make you successful.  What better opportunity than your parents' anniversary to do so.

Lavan was never meant to be a mere ritual where we walk circles around Guru Granth Sahib ji.  Lavan is also not limited to two people getting married.  The purpose of lavan is for a soul to unite with God and in doing so unite with all other souls.  It is a perfect wedding.  If you really wish to do something nice for your parents, please do not organize another ritual.  Instead please do everything you can to get them to understand and live the instructions they received from the Guru in lavan.

You can learn more about the meaning of lavan at:
http://www.srigranth.org/servlet/gurbani.gurbani?Action=Page&Param=773&punjabi=t&id=33099#l33099

You have a wonderful idea, but please execute it they Guru wanted us to.  Even if you are partially successful it would be a wonderful gift for you and all around you.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Tattos
answer:
WJKK
WJKF

As far as I am aware there is nothing written in SGGS per se about the matter. However one needs to look at the reason why someone has a tattoo. There has been a steady increase in the number of people having tattoos since the 1980’s and is more acceptable these days.

My views are as follows:
1] If one has to shave an area before a tattoo is engraved then it is definitely against edicts of Sikhism

2] If one has a tattoo as an allegiance to a particular gang etc. and is a show if pride and arrogance then again it is wrong

3] If the tattoo is used to as a display “for attraction” then again it signifies ਹੌਮੈਂ [egotism] and so is wrong

4] Again there are some people who get "addicted" to having more and more tattoos which again is against Sikh Maryada

5] There are also cases of individuals who have vitiligo and to conceal this they get tattoos. On a personal level I can understand it and have no problems though others may say that it is ਹੌਮੈਂ also

6] If an individual had a tattoo because they were "egged on" by friends then again one can be sympathetic.

7] Of course there are other reasons such as infections, scarring etc why one should not have a tattoo

Gur Fateh

question: The Punjabi/Gurmurki language
answer:
Dear Sister [member],

Please see responses below:

> How do you say in Punjabi/Gurmurki "miracles"?

Commonly used words are: Karamat ਕਰਾਮਾਤ, Chamatkar ਚਮਤਕਾਰ, Sidhi ਸਿੱਧੀ (sidhis are 18 supernatural powers.  These come naturally to people doing naam simran.  Seekers are advised to ignore these powers because they can become a barrier rather than a boon in the path to awareness.)

> Thank you (how do you say Thank you in Punjabi/Gurmurki)

You can say Shukriya or Dhanwaad.

> Has anyone every cried during the Japji Sahib?
> I listened to it & chanted it for the first time today & cried so much. It's so beautiful!

Yes, it happens to the fortunate ones.  Its called 'Bairaag ਬੈਰਾਗੁ' in Gurbani.  Bairaag is a subconscious feeling which makes us feel detached from our surroundings and makes us cry in a longing to meet God, our loved one.
ਸੇ ਗਾਵਹਿ ਜਿਨ ਮਸਤਕਿ ਭਾਗੁ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਭਾਇ ਸਚੈ ਬੈਰਾਗੁ ॥
They alone sing the Lord's Praises, who have such pre-ordained destiny written upon their foreheads, O Siblings of Destiny; through the Love of the True Lord, they find detachment. (SGGS 639).

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh.

question: Saint and professors amongst sikhs
answer:
The designation of Professor is given by the the educational institution where these academics researched and studied hard for their respective post graduate qualification.

The word saint not comparable to sant - sainthood is a title bestowed by the Vatican, and it seems like more and more people such as yourself are intent on catholicising the Sikh path.

Sant in Sikh terms relates to those Gurmukh who have dedicated their lives to first of all learning and later on teaching Gurmat - the word is used correctly amongst the original Sikh sampradas.

SGPC are simply administrators of Gurdwara, they have no power to carry out the above actions, they should focus on establishing education in Gur Ghar and swallowing their pride and sorting out the toilets in Darbaar Sahib and other visited Gurdwarai.

Fortunate few seek the truth and fewer still put the time and energy in searching for a path which is right for them.  Congratulations to you on both the fronts and may Guru be with you always.

question: How to react if you get insulted?
answer:
Great question. This is my understanding:
No this is not in Hukam. When people have Naam, they act in Hukam and for a person to be insulting another, for them to act in ego, for them to hurt another means they do not have Naam and therefore it is not in Hukam.

Secondly, it kind of depends on setting but the important part is controlling your own emotions so that you definitely don’t hit them, don’t yell at them and don’t insult back! You want to do your best not to be angry back. Honestly it’s the 5 thieves in each person- lust, anger, greed, attachment, and pride, plus ego that make people insult others. And when the 5 in you start fighting with the 5 in them, you lose out the time that you could have spent in peace meditating on God and living happily. You lose precious breath and you spend it in maya. I know it can hurt when we are insulted, particularly if we have not meditated enough to be at a spiritual level at which we can ignore what people say about us. The ultimate goal is to do enough simran and reach that level so that it doesn’t matter what other people think of you- whether it is praise or insult, it doesn’t matter. In the meantime though I personally like to remember that people’s insults comes from their own jealousy or pain often and that it’s best to just keep moving forward gracefully. I have reacted in anger on occasion and I feel rotten afterwards. It’s awful and I don’t recommend it. Take from example of Guru Jis who were insulted, who had people throwing rocks at them and insulting them, and yet they did not react back in the same manner.

Sometimes the situation will deem you need to be silent- that does not necessarily mean you are ignoring it. Two people can’t fight if one doesn’t engage. Sometimes the situation will mean being direct and saying that their language is not acceptable. For example I had someone swearing at me in my workplace and I had a colleague simply say “we do not tolerate abusive language in this workplace.” It was a great response which I have memorized for next time. You can stand up for yourself, but you don’t need to respond in anger. Make sure you are in control of your thoughts.

One who is beyond praise and slander, one who considers gold and iron as same, Nanak says , listen mind , he is image of God.

This is the stage of a BRAHAMGYANI. W e need to strive to be at that stage by meditation, gurbani reading and sewa. Else it will be just thoughts. Just a smile.

question: Etiquette advice for non Sikh attending death celebration
answer:
Hello & welcome to Sikhnet.

I would like to suggest that you wear cream, beige, grey or some dull colour top.

Red & other bright colours are generally avoided at mourning.

Grey or black plain scarf is more appropriate than a decorated one.

It is best that you stay with your friend & help her out.

When you are alone sit with the congregation.
See where & how other women are sitting then follow suit.

As for greetings "Sat Sri Akal" or Hello would do.

Lastly just be yourself & support your friend.

question: Etiquette advice for non Sikh attending death celebration
answer:
Just posting my thoughts post ceremony service for reference to others who may find themselves in a similar position in the future. I will note that it's possible other Gurdwara's are different

Dress
I found that there were many people dressed in brightly coloured clothing with fancy beaded head scarves, including direct relatives, as opposed to those who were general members of the congregation. I shouldn't have worried about this. My friend's mother wore blue, her aunt pink. There was also a box full of scarves to wear to cover your head once you'd deposited your shoes and I was able to find one that was dark coloured easily.

General
Everyone was extremely welcoming and helpful when I asked them. I did feel a bit awkward entering the main prayer hall on my own (my friend was elsewhere when I arrived) due to unfamiliarity but was made to feel very welcome seated next to strangers until my friend arrived and introduced me to the wider family who I sat with for the rest of the service.

Those more familiar with Christian worship services will maybe find it strange that people to leave for an occasional break to go to the bathroom, etc. but this seemed to be perfectly normal to do.

After the service finished everyone joined together to have lunch and, for me, this was a beautiful experience. It was a chance to talk about my friend's dad and the positive things he'd brought to her and her family but also to share with other community members who were happy to explain aspects of the faith. I was genuinely taken by how unpretentious and welcoming everyone was.

It was a tough day for my friend and her family but she got through it and gave a great speech about her dad in Punjabi that had everyone in tears because it was from the heart. So proud of her. And her dad would be too.

[member], thanks for your advice: you were very right: the best thing was to just be there and support her, something that will never stop.

question: Shabad's Meaning
answer:
ਸਿਰੀਰਾਗੁ ਮਹਲਾ ੩ ॥
Siree Raag, Third Mehl ||

ਕਿਸੁ ਹਉ ਸੇਵੀ ਕਿਆ ਜਪੁ ਕਰੀ ਸਤਗੁਰ ਪੂਛਉ ਜਾਇ ॥
When I ask my Guru, whom shall I serve and what meditation shall I recite?
ਸਤਗੁਰ ਕਾ ਭਾਣਾ ਮੰਨਿ ਲਈ ਵਿਚਹੁ ਆਪੁ ਗਵਾਇ ॥
 [The advice is] I need to eradicate selfishness from within and accept the Will of the True Guru
ਏਹਾ ਸੇਵਾ ਚਾਕਰੀ ਨਾਮੁ ਵਸੈ ਮਨਿ ਆਇ ॥
By this work and service, The Lord’s Name will come to dwell within my mind
ਨਾਮੈ ਹੀ ਤੇ ਸੁਖੁ ਪਾਈਐ ਸਚੈ ਸਬਦਿ ਸੁਹਾਇ ॥੧॥
Through the Lord’s Name, peace is obtained; and I am adorned by the True Shabad [God’s Word/Command] ||1||
ਮਨ ਮੇਰੇ ਅਨਦਿਨੁ ਜਾਗੁ ਹਰਿ ਚੇਤਿ ॥
O my mind! always be aware [i.e. of the influence of Maya and vices] and recite the Lord’s Name
ਆਪਣੀ ਖੇਤੀ ਰਖਿ ਲੈ ਕੂੰਜ ਪੜੈਗੀ ਖੇਤਿ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ ॥
Protect your crops [i.e. protect one’s spiritual life from Maya and vices]] or the crane [migratory bird {synonymous to old age}] will descend on your farm [i.e. your life will be eaten away by Maya and Vices] ||1||Pause||
ਮਨ ਕੀਆ ਇਛਾ ਪੂਰੀਆ ਸਬਦਿ ਰਹਿਆ ਭਰਪੂਰਿ ॥
Those who are filled to overflowing [i.e. meditate upon] by the Shabad [God’s Word/Command] have the wishes of their mind fulfilled [i.e. are no longer influenced by Maya and the vices]
ਭੈ ਭਾਇ ਭਗਤਿ ਕਰਹਿ ਦਿਨੁ ਰਾਤੀ ਹਰਿ ਜੀਉ ਵੇਖੈ ਸਦਾ ਹਦੂਰਿ ॥
One who is in deference to the Lord, loves and is devoted to Him day and night; sees the Dear Lord always close at hand
ਸਚੈ ਸਬਦਿ ਸਦਾ ਮਨੁ ਰਾਤਾ ਭ੍ਰਮੁ ਗਇਆ ਸਰੀਰਹੁ ਦੂਰਿ ॥
Their minds remain forever imbued in the colours of the True Shabad [God’s Word/Command] and doubts are erased from their bodies
ਨਿਰਮਲੁ ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਪਾਇਆ ਸਾਚਾ ਗੁਣੀ ਗਹੀਰੁ ॥੨॥
They find the Immaculate Lord and Master. He is True, He is the Treasure of Qualities ||2||
ਜੋ ਜਾਗੇ ਸੇ ਉਬਰੇ ਸੂਤੇ ਗਏ ਮੁਹਾਇ ॥
Those who remain awake [to influences of Maya and vices] are saved, while those who sleep are plundered [i.e. lose their spiritual life]
ਸਚਾ ਸਬਦੁ ਨ ਪਛਾਣਿਓ ਸੁਪਨਾ ਗਇਆ ਵਿਹਾਇ ॥
They do not recognise the True Shabad [God’s Word/Command] and like a dream, their lives fade away [are wasted]
ਸੁੰਞੇ ਘਰ ਕਾ ਪਾਹੁਣਾ ਜਿਉ ਆਇਆ ਤਿਉ ਜਾਇ ॥
Like guests in a deserted house, they leave just as they have come [i.e. they depart from this world empty handed]
ਮਨਮੁਖ ਜਨਮੁ ਬਿਰਥਾ ਗਇਆ ਕਿਆ ਮੁਹੁ ਦੇਸੀ ਜਾਇ ॥੩॥
The life of the non-believer is useless. What face will he show when he goes from here? [i.e. dies and goes to the Lord’s Court] ||3||
ਸਭ ਕਿਛੁ ਆਪੇ ਆਪਿ ਹੈ ਹਉਮੈ ਵਿਚਿ ਕਹਨੁ ਨ ਜਾਇ ॥
God Himself is everything; those entangled in ego cannot even speak of this [i.e. do not understand that whatever happens is by His Will]
ਗੁਰ ਕੈ ਸਬਦਿ ਪਛਾਣੀਐ ਦੁਖੁ ਹਉਮੈ ਵਿਚਹੁ ਗਵਾਇ ॥
It is through the Guru’s Shabad [God’s Word/Command] , He is realised and the pain of egotism is eradicated from within
ਸਤਗੁਰੁ ਸੇਵਨਿ ਆਪਣਾ ਹਉ ਤਿਨ ਕੈ ਲਾਗਉ ਪਾਇ ॥
I fall at the feet of those [i.e. I venerate them and try to follow their example] who serve their True Guru [i.e. follow His Teachings]
ਨਾਨਕ ਦਰਿ ਸਚੈ ਸਚਿਆਰ ਹਹਿ ਹਉ ਤਿਨ ਬਲਿਹਾਰੈ ਜਾਉ ॥੪॥੨੧॥੫੪॥
O Nanak! I am a sacrifice to those [i.e. reveres them] who are found to be true [i.e. genuine] in the True Court ||4||21||54||

question: Want To Convert
answer: Well, to become a Sikh, you just need to go to Gurduara and do prayer in front of Guru Granth Sahib and bow down and accept that you accept the teachings. Then you start learning and applying. This will take a while. When you living standard improves and you live according to teachings, your family shall see the change in you and might take interest on why. This will help you let them know. The basic is refraining from 4 bajjar kurehits to start. They are available in the Sikh Code of Conduct. If you want to become a Khalsa, then you must adhere to the strict code for Khalsa which is a bit more difficult. Gurbani translations are available online and you can read but I will say that they aren't 100% accurate translations but they are good enough if you just want to get started and get learning.

question: Newbie wanting to learn more about Sikhi
answer:
[member],

Welcome to the forum.  Sikhism entails following the logical path laid out by the Guru for our own betterment.  On this path, we  slowly control  our mind's coercive powers which push us on a destructive, self-centered and indulgent path.  A good path is a good path regardless of one's religion or spiritual stage.  Therefore, what is good for an amritdhari is also good for any Sikh or for any human being.  By taking amrit, we are simply pledging our commitment to do things which we should have always been doing.

Alcohol is prohibited in Sikhism, and the Guru has given logical reasons why alcohol or any other intoxicant should be avoided (SGGS 554).

Eating meat is not prohibited for a Sikh or an amritdhari.  There are some sub-groups within Sikhism who refuse to baptize a person without a pledge to stop eating meat.  However, there is no such requirement in Sikh Rehat Maryada (SRM), the most widely accepted code of the Sikhs.  What is prohibited is any ritualistic killing or adopting a belief that somehow a ritual would remove bad karma from a food.  Having said this, the Guru wants us to avoid any type of food which is not good for our health or spiritual well being.  My personal belief is that meat is not the best diet for most of us who have access to good and balanced vegetarian options.

One thing to note is that Sikhism is a sehaj path (meaning a gentle path of continuous improvement rather than a jolt which would turn a person's life upside down).  The Guru says that if we keep climbing a ladder one step at a time, we will eventually reach the Lord (SGGS 7).  So best thing is to keep taking stock of our actions and one by one change those actions which are not in accordance with the Guru's wishes.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Karma
answer:
What is Karma?

The scientific concept of cause and effect, action and reaction is called the law of Karma(in religious parlance). A man reaps what he sows. Is it not typical that in spite of the law of Karma, man expects nectar after sowing poison?

Just as our present life is the result of our past Karma, the present Karma will determine our future life. Karma operates in this life and succesive ones. The law of Karma does not cease to operate after death, because death is just a matter of physical disintegration, and has no effect on the soul, which survives.

God is the Creator of the first Karma, the origin of the universe, and the destroyer of Karma.

Good or evil by frequent repetition leave their impression on character. A man doing wicked deeds continuously will turn into a bad character. This produces states of mind, like anxiety, fear and guilt, all of which will cause pain and suffering to the individual.

Karma does not mean that everything is pre-ordained and that man has no free-will. He carries his past Karma in the form of character. It is his own actions that make him what he is. Guru Nanak says, "The record of my deeds cannot be effaced because God has recorded them." Man has to sow seeds, the choice and the initiative to certain extent. He also has the ability to change the course of events even though circumscribed by heredity and environment. God as the Ruler of the Universe controls the over-all destiny of individual. Like the prodigal son, sinners turn to Him only as the last resort.

Sikhism modified the theory of Karma in two directions. Firstly, efforts of the individual are necessary for improving his own condition. Man is responsible for his lot. He must not blame God for his destiny. He must think of the present and the future. Secondly, Karma can be changed by prayer and the Grace of God.

When an individual learns to submit to His will, he ceases to make new Karma. He offers all his actions to Him; he acts as the instrument of His Will. According to Sikhism, all past Karma may then be erased through the association with saints, and meditation on "The Name".

question: responsibilities of daughter

Sons of farmers inherited land and in return took care of their parents in old age. Daughters were married away with responsibly to help their husbands, who inherited paternal land, and in turn must take care of their parents. As we move forward some of the traditions mentioned above are being challenged. Rightfully so!

question: Guru Ramdas  Sahib ji de Gurpurab di lakh lakh wadhayee
answer:
Waheguru ji ka khalsa
Waheguru ji ki fateh

Guru Ramdas Sahib ji de aagaman purab di beant vadhai hoveh ji.

"Samrath guru sir hath dharyao.   Gur kini kirpa har nam diao jis dekh charann aghann haryao.   Nis basur ek saman dhian so nam sune sut bhan daryao."

The All-powerful Guru placed His hand upon my head. The Guru was kind, and blessed me with the Lord's Name. Gazing upon His Feet, my sins were dispelled. Night and day, the Guru meditates on the One Lord; hearing His Name, the Messenger of Death is scared away.

ਸਮਰੱਥ ਗੁਰੂ (ਅਮਰਦਾਸ ਜੀ) ਨੇ (ਗੁਰੂ ਰਾਮਦਾਸ ਜੀ ਦੇ) ਸਿਰ ਉੱਤੇ ਹੱਥ ਰੱਖਿਆ ਹੈ। ਜਿਸ (ਗੁਰੂ ਅਮਰਦਾਸ ਜੀ) ਦੇ ਚਰਨਾਂ ਦਾ ਦਰਸ਼ਨ ਕੀਤਿਆਂ ਪਾਪ ਦੂਰ ਹੋ ਜਾਂਦੇ ਹਨ, ਉਸ ਗੁਰੂ ਨੇ ਮਿਹਰ ਕੀਤੀ ਹੈ, (ਗੁਰੂ ਰਾਮਦਾਸ ਜੀ ਨੂੰ) ਹਰੀ ਦਾ ਨਾਮ ਬਖ਼ਸ਼ਿਆ ਹੈ; (ਉਸ ਨਾਮ ਵਿਚ ਗੁਰੂ ਰਾਮਦਾਸ ਜੀ ਦਾ) ਦਿਨ ਰਾਤ ਇੱਕ-ਰਸ ਧਿਆਨ ਰਹਿੰਦਾ ਹੈ, ਉਸ ਨਾਮ ਦੇ ਸੁਣਨ ਨਾਲ ਜਮ-ਰਾਜ (ਭੀ) ਡਰਦਾ ਹੈ (ਭਾਵ, ਨੇੜੇ ਨਹੀਂ ਆਉਂਦਾ)।
