question: Forgotten tradition followed among Hindu families
answer:
Even though I have heard about it many times, I highly doubt that it was as widespread tradition as touted. Good thing about Sikh history is that it's not too old where facts cannot be verified.

If this practice was indeed widespread 50 years ago, we will see many Sikhs whose grandparents or great grandparents were Hindus. But we rarely see such phenomenon. In post Guruship period, most of Sikh population increased during Maharaja Ranjit Singh's times. After British took over Punjab, there was strong emphasis on Christianity and converting Sikhs/Hindus to Christianity. With the arrival of Arya Samaj around 1870s, and hateful comments from it's leader 'Swami' Dayanand, rift between Hindus and Sikhs continued to grow. Singh Sabha movement which also started at the same time stressed more upon distinct practices and identity of Sikhism. Therefore, I hardly see a period where most Hindu families made their first son a Sikh.

On the other hand, there are plenty of examples of Hindus who did convert to Sikhism and did so on their own. Some of them became very well known Sikhs in the history. Bhagat Puran Singh, Prof. Sahib Singh etc. are few examples of such conversions.

question: Forgotten tradition followed among Hindu families
answer:
I think this tradition was not common among Hindus at large as often propagated but mainly among Sahejdhari sikhs. Who had their strong belief in Guru Granth Sahib and ten Gurus. Occasionally, a family would decide to get one of their children baptised as Singh. It largely depended on the level of preaching of Gurmat in a particular area. For intance, the large Sahejdhari Khatri population in the Pothohar are of Punjab around Rawalpindi during the late 1800's and early 1900's converted to full blown Sikhi under the influence of Sant Baba Attar Singh of Mastuana (for instance, Master Tara Singh) or earlier under the influence of Bedi preachers like Baba Khem Singh Bedi would get one child baptised as Sikh. Once a family member was thus baptised this tradition would continue in later generations. In such families, a formally sikh person would marry a bride from a hindu family in the same caste. This was quite common and still is among for instance, Arora families and several other groups.

Humbly

question: Sahajdhari Marg
answer:
[member] Ji,

Firstly we must not think of the Gurus as being separate entities, they were the same Jyote in successive bodies. The jyote was the same,
hence the mission was the same, and Guru Gobind Singh Ji’s final form given to the Sikhs was a culmination of all that the Gurus had prepared the ground for.
So there is really no picking a choosing what you like and what you don’t like, when looked at deeply it is all the same message.

The Janayo was seen as a way of worshipping God by the people, the thinking was that if you wore the ganayo then you were worshipping God and Guru Nanak Dev Ji said that this was incorrect because if the ganayo break then does you worshipping break ? or does you faith in God break? This was in the same vein as people offering water to the sun thinking it would reach their ancestors or the ritual of Saraadh which is offerings to the ancestors.

Firstly the Kakars give a sense of order and belonging and remember the Khalsa was created at a time of turmoil so it has its roots in the martial tradition which leads to the Rehat or code of conduct that gives its followers discipline and a moral code. and they are for all people not just for the high priest or privileged classes.The kakars have a purpose, the kirpan, the kashera, the unshorn hair all have a purpose and significance. It is the  beginning on the road to nirvana, but  you do not get enlightenment just by wearing them, there us a long road ahead.  Guru Nanak Dev Ji created Sant and Guru Gobind Singh Ji transformed them into Sant Sapahi. You could say that Sant Sapahi were needed at the time as there was such lawlessness and upheaval but Guru Ji in His foresightedness created the Khalsa for always. We need to be disciplined and we need a moral compass and we need to follow a rehat / code of conduct.

Guru Ji once gave the hukam that no Khalsa shall even touch a turkwoman, on the face of it one may say why? What is wrong with them? Are they considered dirty or beneath us? But looking deeper the reason was to adhere the Khalsa to a higher ideal, to keep them with the highest of morals. At the time it was open season by the invaders on the indigenous women population and atrocities were committed against them on a daily basis and Guru Ji did not want His Khalsa to follow suit and retaliate in kind, He wanted His Khalsa to stick to a high moral code and regard all women as his sisters or daughters. The message is the same, from Guru Nanak Dev Ji to Guru Gobind Singh Ji.

question: Punjabi Translation
answer:
Sat Sri Akal

> Mahh boothh tanvad haa? Is that it?

JI, I expect different dialects  in the various parts of the Punjab will lead to slight variations.

As far as I am aware, and based on  my own common usage, I would say  "shukhrhiaa" when expressing simple "thanks", or "thanvaddhi" for "thank you".

When it comes to saying something like, "I am grateful to you", or "I am obliged to you", I would say "Meh apne thanvaaadi hai",  or "Meh apne thanvaaadi han", or even "Meh thanvaadi hai/han "  (ie omit apne) the "i" sound after the thanvaad gets across the meaning that the thanks is "to somebody" ; if you are in conversation with one other person or one group,  you would not need to say apne,  as it would be expected that your thanks are to that person or to that whole group and you are not passing your thanks to a third person/group.

I think  "han" would be used when writing rather than "hai" ; I have heard people say "han"  but I read it more often, (I can't actually read much at all as my knowledge of Gurmukhi is very limited )  and I personally would use "hai" when speaking,  but like I said at the beginning, just "shukhrhiaa" is sufficient to say "thanks".  You might want to follow it with "ji", to increase the politeness, and I do.

"bohth" is akin to saying "very"  ie  used when saying  "I am very grateful to you", instead of "I am grateful to you"

Good luck in your progress

question: what is SURAT SHABD YOGA?
answer:
SURAT SHABD YOGA -

meeting of  GURU NANAK dev ji  with  yogis at  achal sahib near  batala   ( gurdaspur )  from  siddh gosht  ( guru granth sahib ji )

yogis asked  various  questions from   guru nanak dev ji .

one question

   kavan  guru  ji ka tu chela  ?
Who is your guru? Whose disciple are you?

guru nanak dev ji replied

 shabd guru ,surat   dhun cheela

ie my  guru  is shabd (true words ),and  my surat ( consciousness )follows it

listening shabd is also described as  anahad naad ( unstruck melody ) , ajappa  jaap  .

 below is an article   which touched  your all questions on this forum

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

AJAPA JAAP (continuos repetition of Naam/ Waheguru) is the spiritual condition of a person when the Simran (repitition of Waheguru) goes on an auto pilot mode in your Surat (mind) and in your Hirdey (heart) as explained below. It means that Simran becomes a round the clock thing inside you, Simran doesn’t stop at any moment, it carries on and such a condition comes with Gurkirpa (God/ the guru’s blessing) and after a lot of Bhagti Kamai(meditation) or can also be attained with the Kirpa (blessings) of a Puran Braham Gyani(ascended master). The experiences of bliss follow a path such as this:

1. Jaap (repetition) with Tounge – Rasna – this happens in Dharam Khand

2. Jaap with the breathing – with Swaas – this happens in Gyan Khand and Saram Khand

3. Then Naam (waheguru) goes into your mind – Surat, in your thinking, then it becomes
Simran from Jaap – this is a very good stage – this happens in Saram Khand and
Karam Khand.

4. The next stage is when Simran goes into Hirdey – this one is even much higher stage
when Naam goes into Hirdey – this is where it goes on an automatic mode, this is
where the real bhagti(meditation) starts.

5. The next stage is when Simran travels to the Nabhi, when Nabhi
Kamal(lotus)blossoms – Karam Khand

6. The next Stage is when Simran goes into Kundlini – Mooladhaar Chakkar and spine –
Karam Khand

7. The next stage is when Simran travels through the spine to the brain, and back to Surat where it completes the cycle.

This is what the real Mala (rosary) of Naam (meditation) is. When this happens then the Gyan Netter and Dassam Duaar (10th Gate) open s and you form a permanent connection with Akal Purakh (God), you start to receive divine knowledge – “Braham Gyan”. This happens in Sach Khand. Enjoyment – Anand in Smadhi and Sun Smadhi is beyond description. That is why the enlightened souls go into v ery deep meditation some time for days together. You experience a lot of things during your Smadhi and Sun Smadhi, see a lot of things, meet a lot of Saints, Gurus, see Param Jyot, conversation with the Sants and Akal Purakh , it is beyond description wh at happens and through what you go when you go into deep meditation. This is the stage when all the doors – Bajjar Kapaat are opened and there is a continuous flow of Amrit, body is always full of Amrit.

8. The Simran in Smadhi and Sun Smadhi continues until NIRGUN AND SARGUN
becomes one, at this point Simran goes into rom-rom – every bit of your body does
Naam Simran, your Suksham Dehi becomes as pure as gold, your entire body is filled
with Naam Amrit all the time. You become Braham Leen, and reach Atal Awastha.
These stages are beyond description. Sat Chit Anand Ghar Hamare – Gurmukh Rom
Rom Har Dhyae – Nirgun Sargun Nirankaar Sun Smadhi Aap, Apan Kia Nanka Apan
Hi Fir Jaap and so on. One lives in Pu ran Parkash all the time and listens to Ilahi
Kirtan(heavenly Kirtan/singing)– Anhad Naad Dhunis (heavenly music) all the time. It
is just incredible experience. This is when one becomes Sat Ram Dass and is directed
by the Almighty to serve humanity in h umbleness. And this is what we all wish to
achieve being fortunate enough to move on the Bhagti Marg (spiritual path).

If you do Jaap with Rasna your Rasna will become pavitter - pious, by doing jaap in along breathing - swass your swass will become pious - pavitter, by doing Simran in mind-Surat-Chit- mind will become pious - pavitter (pure), and that is what you need t o do to make your mind pious - pavitter, that is how you will have control on your mind - MAN JEETE JAG JEET (win teh mind and you win the world) - MAN TU JYOT SAROOP HAI and you will be able to rise above Panj Doots - KAAM, KRODH, LOBH, MOH, AHANKAAR AN D ALSO ASA, TRISHNA, MANSHA, NINDYA, CHUGLI, BAKHILI, RAJ, JOBAN, DHAN, MAAL, ROOP, RAS, GANDH, THESE THUGS – MENTAL SICKNESSES, and when Simran goes in to Hirdey - and Simran will go to Hirdey by itself with Gurkirpa (guru’s blessings) only, and so in C hit, Hirdey will become pavitter - pious and a pious Hirdey will become Mahaparupkari and Dana Dina, NIRBHAO, NIRVAIR and so on, it will start to absorb all the vital qualities of Akal Purakh (god) and will become a Puran Sant Hirda, and will achieve JIV AN MUKTI.

answer:
Aadays Tasai Aadays
Āḏes ṯisai āḏes.
I bow to Him, I humbly bow.

Āḏ anīl anāḏ anāhaṯ jug jug eko ves. ||28||
The Primal One, the Pure Light, without beginning, without end. Throughout all the ages, He is One and the Same. ||28||

Bẖugaṯ gi▫ān ḏa▫i▫ā bẖandāraṇ gẖat gẖat vājėh nāḏ.
Let spiritual wisdom be your food, and compassion your attendant. The Sound-current of the Naad vibrates in each and every heart.

Āp nāth nāthī sabẖ jā kī riḏẖ siḏẖ avrā sāḏ.
He Himself is the Supreme Master of all; wealth and miraculous spiritual powers, and all other external tastes and pleasures, are all like beads on a string.

Sanjog vijog ḏu▫e kār cẖalāvėh lekẖe āvahi bẖāg.
Union with Him, and separation from Him, come by His Will. We come to receive what is written in our destiny.

2 RAY MAN

ਰੇ ਮਨ ਇਹਿ ਬਿਧਿ ਜੋਗੁ ਕਮਾਓ ॥
रे मन इहि बिधि जोगु कमाओ ॥
O Mind ! the Yoga be practised in this way :

ਸਿੰਙੀ ਸਾਚ ਅਕਪਟ ਕੰਠਲਾ ਧਿਆਨ ਬਿਭੂਤ ਚੜ੍ਹਾਓ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ ॥
सिंङी साच अकपट कंठला धिआन बिभूत चड़्हाओ ॥१॥ रहाउ ॥
Consider the Truth as the horn, sincerity the necklace and meditation as ashes to be applied to your body…...Pause.

ਤਾਤੀ ਗਹੁ ਆਤਮ ਬਸਿ ਕਰ ਕੀ ਭਿੱਛਾ ਨਾਮ ਅਧਾਰੰ ॥
ताती गहु आतम बसि कर की भि्छा नाम अधारं ॥
Make self-control your lyre and the prop of the Name as your alms,

ਬਾਜੇ ਪਰਮ ਤਾਰ ਤਤੁ ਹਰਿ ਕੋ ਉਪਜੈ ਰਾਗ ਰਸਾਰੰ ॥੧॥
बाजे परम तार ततु हरि को उपजै राग रसारं ॥१॥
Then the supreme essence will be played like the main string creating savoury divine music.1.

ਉਘਟੈ ਤਾਨ ਤਰੰਗ ਰੰਗਿ ਅਤਿ ਗਯਾਨ ਗੀਤ ਬੰਧਾਨੰ ॥
उघटै तान तरंग रंगि अति गयान गीत बंधानं ॥
The wave of colourful tune will arise, manifesting the song of knowledge,

ਚਕਿ ਚਕਿ ਰਹੇ ਦੇਵ ਦਾਨਵ ਮੁਨਿ ਛਕਿ ਛਕਿ ਬਯੋਮ ਬਿਵਾਨੰ ॥੨॥
चकि चकि रहे देव दानव मुनि छकि छकि बयोम बिवानं ॥२॥
The gods, demons and sages would be amazed enjoying their ride in heavenly chariots.2.

ਆਤਮ ਉਪਦੇਸ਼ ਭੇਸੁ ਸੰਜਮ ਕੋ ਜਾਪੁ ਸੁ ਅਜਪਾ ਜਾਪੇ ॥
आतम उपदेश भेसु संजम को जापु सु अजपा जापे ॥
While instructing the self in the garb of self-restraint and reciting God`s Name inwardly,

ਸਦਾ ਰਹੈ ਕੰਚਨ ਸੀ ਕਾਯਾ ਕਾਲ ਨ ਕਬਹੂੰ ਬਯਾਪੇ ॥੩॥੨॥
सदा रहै कंचन सी काया काल न कबहूं बयापे ॥३॥२॥
The body will always remain like gold and become immortal.3.2.

"People staring at me is the least I’ve faced growing up as a Sikh in America. People stare at me all the time. There is no where on this earth except my hometwon Gurdwara where people don’t stare at me. My childhood challenged me in many ways, relating to my appearance. My brother and I were the only Sikh AND the only Anglo students in our school. People used to pick on us and fight with us and threaten us. I spent the first 18 years of my life facing the abuse of unaccepting individuals with difficulty. When I became an adult I chose not to be a victim anymore.
Society may never accept me, but my Guru accepts me. I would rather die the son of Guru Gobind Singh than live a life of cowardice. I would rather face a hundred more years of abuse than give up the image that my spiritual father bestowed upon me.
If people making fun of your eyebrows is too much of a price to pay for being a Sikh of the Guru, I would ask that you remember all the shaheeds who gave their life before their hair.
It is not a burden to live as Khalsa, it is a gift! It is a burdent to live by the standards of others. Our Guru gave us the highest standard which, a timeles standard. We recognize “Akal Moorat” the image of the undying. Honoring our bodies as God made them is honoring God within us. Guru Ji says that God is “hazaraa hazoor” (Ever present and present everywhere). God is within each individual eyebrow, why pluck them because of people who cannot see that? “If you cannot see God in All, you cannot see God at all.” - By Prabhu Singh in an article on mrsikhnet.com when revealing the purpose of wearing full bana

question: SOS Transliteration
answer:
> Sat Nam,
> Many Blessings and peace to you all
> While reading the SGGS i have some troubles on how to say the numbers, in the transliteration of SGGS they only put the number and not how to say it, for example: "Ramkhalee Mehla 3" So my question is how to say the nombers?
> I know that 1 is "pehlaa" and number 3 is "teeja" right?
>
> Moderator Comment: Right. This is indicated at some places in SGGS.

Many people do pronounce the numbers wrong. Please also do not and a "an" sound at the end. What I mean by is do not add a nasal sound, the bindi at the end.

1 - Pehla (make sure you have the peh sound, not pai)
2 - Dooja
3 - Teeja
4- Chaudha (have the ਥ sound in the "dha" part)
5 - Panjva
6 - Shayva
7 - Satva
8 - Attva (in the "tt" have a ਠ sound)
9 - Naava (This is not pronounce Nauvan, but Naava)

There's much more after this, but I haven't taken that much santhiya to actually know how to properly pronounce those numbers.

question: Prayers
answer:
[member] Ji, do not worry you are doing really good.

The idea is to remember Guru Ji / God (same thing) all the time - Swaas swaas simro Gobind - Remember God with every breath you take. You are trying to do this by doing paath / Simran as part of your daily routine so you are doing really well, so well done !

There is nothing wrong in reading gurbani from cell phone or screen, so you are okay there.
If you break off to take calls, no problem, just start where you left off, so you are okay there.
If you want to take of your shoes and wash you hands that is great, if you cannot then that is okay also.
Obviously when you do paath at home then you can do it properly with bare feet and head covered and clean hands etc, but at work or when you are going about your daily life then just keep doing your paath keep doing your Simran.
You may think should I be doing paath in the bath room or when I am out and about? Answer is , absolutely , God is everywhere and you can remember Him everywhere, the secret is to build your relationship with your True Father and what better then to remember Him while you are working.

So, don't worry and carry on your good path.

ਜਿਨ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਜਿਨ ਹਰਿ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਧਿਆਇਆ ਜੀ ਤਿਨ ਕਾ ਭਉ ਸਭੁ ਗਵਾਸੀ ॥
जिन निरभउ जिन हरि निरभउ धिआइआ जी तिन का भउ सभु गवासी ॥
Jin nirbha▫o jin har nirbha▫o dhi▫ā▫i▫ā jī tin kā bha▫o sabh gavāsī.
Those who meditate on the Fearless One, on the Fearless Lord-all their fears are dispelled.

ਭਉ ਸਭੁ = ਸਾਰਾ ਡਰ। ਗਵਾਸੀ = ਦੂਰ ਕਰ ਦੇਂਦਾ ਹੈ।

ਜਿਨ੍ਹਾਂ ਬੰਦਿਆਂ ਨੇ ਸਦਾ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਪ੍ਰਭੂ ਦਾ ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਿਆ ਹੈ; ਪ੍ਰਭੂ ਉਹਨਾਂ ਦਾ ਸਾਰਾ ਡਰ ਦੂਰ ਕਰ ਦੇਂਦਾ ਹੈ।

Source: http://www.srigranth.org/servlet/gurbani.gurbani?Action=Page&Param=11&g=1&h=1&r=1&t=1&p=0&k=1

A Sikh is advised to fear God and obey God’s command's. One who obeys these orders he emulates the Divine virtue of fearlessness, as he has nothing to fear. Guru Granth Sahib jeeo is replete with exhortations to submit to the will of God and fear in the creative sense, which is fear of the highest authority God. A few examples are as follows

- Seek the sanctuary of the highest authority above whom there is none.

- O unvigilant man be afraid of committing sin, Seek refuge in the compassionate Lord who dispels all fear.

- When one fears doing wrong, this gets imbedded in the mind and then there is no other fear.

- The way to avoid fear at the work place is to identify with the objectives of the employer.

- And finally, fear of the Lord leads to love for Him.

ਗਉੜੀ  ਮਹਲਾ  ੫  ॥
गउड़ी महला ५ ॥
Ga▫oṛī mėhlā 5.

ਦੁਸਟ ਦੂਤ ਪਰਮੇਸਰਿ ਮਾਰੇ ॥

ਬਾਦਿਸਾਹ ਸਾਹ ਸਭ ਵਸਿ ਕਰਿ ਦੀਨੇ ॥

question: The Nihangs are pathetic
answer:
Waheguru ji ka khalsa
Waheguru ji ki fateh

I was in Amritsar city during the Blue Star period. At the time Baba Santa Singh was supervising the Akal Takhat rebuilding on behalf of Indira Gandhi I saw Santa Singh going along the prikarma of Darbar Sahib on foot in a hot and humid weather but a couple of his followers followed him carrying behind him a thing called 'Room Cooler" ( a poor person's substitute for air conditioner) that is a tin box about a meter cube with an arrangement to throw cool air cooled by dripping water on a grass mat inside using a large fan inside the box . There were a few of the Nihang 'sevadars' of Santa Singh carrying a very very long electric cable through which the 'Room Cooler' was plugged to an electric socket somewhere. Normally, as a cultural tradition in old times, a Chaur would be waved on the head of the religious or political leader. However, this was the height of stupidity to substitute a 'Chaur' or a hand fan, that too in the pricincts of Darbar Sahib, and using such foolish arrangement. That speaks also for those who wish to imitate 'Budha Dal' traditions. Incidentally, the real 'Budha Dal' got dissolved in mid eighteenth century when the Misls got firmly established.

Humbly
[member]

extra.question_body:
Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh!

Many Sikhs in the modern day revere the Akali Nihangs, a Sikh martial order which asserts its status as 'Gur Kee Ladlee Fauj', the Guru's beloved army. Many of us also imitate their dress, tie dumallas as they do and adorn them with chakars and chand toray. But personally, I find the Nihangs to be the utter antithesis of devoutness, a blot on the Khalsa Panth.

In the census report for the Punjab, 1881, Sir Denzel Ibbetson writes,"When Sikhism was politically dominant, the Akālis were accustomed to extort alms by accusing the principal chiefs (Sikh misldars) of crimes, imposing fines upon them, and in the event of their refusing to pay, preventing them from performing their ablutions or going through any of the religious ceremonies at Amritsar.” When one visits Nihang websites, they are bombarded with tales of how Nihangs exploited their position as the 'Guru's beloved army' to simply take whatever they wished, when they felt like it.

By following this link ([link]) to the paragraph at the very bottom of the page, it may be understood that the Nihangs were notoriously intolerant, lawless, and again took advantage of the positions afforded to them by their title of 'Guru's beloved army'.

In modern times, the authority of the Nihangs has been significantly undermined, and they have an almost negligible influence over Sikh affairs. They try especially hard to regain the position that they held under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, once again arguing that they are the 'Guru's beloved army' and the protectors of Sikhism. My question to the nihangs is this:

If you are really the protectors of Sikhi, then where were you in 1984, and in the years following, when the Sikhs you claim to protect were being butchered by the thousands?

Our 'protectors' were sitting in their camps getting high on bhang dawn till dusk. The Budha Dal Jathedar, Santa Singh, undertook a Kar Seva of Akal Takhat, on behalf of the Indian government, who had butchered the very same Sikhs the Nihangs claim to protect.  Read about it here: "[link]"

An article by the Indian Journalist Chand Joshi reaffirms this:

“Finally like a lottery ticket, from Pandora’s box the Government got hold of a Nihang chief called Santa Singh (the government were looking for a Sikh to undertake Kar Seva on their behalf) who could neither claim the religious puritanism of Bhindranwale or the mass following of any of the political leaders, but called himself the leader of “86 crores”. *

Armed opium-drinking followers of the newly discovered “saint” then began a much publicised Kar Seva which far from mollifying Sikh feeling only helped in accelerating the feeling of hurt. Baba Santa Singh became a new spokesman who vitiated the atmosphere, but a person nevertheless considered from deck-chairs in Delhi to be the central point in the “healing process” which Prime Minister Indira Gandhi had called for immediately after the action in the Golden Temple.”

Gurdarshan Singh Dhillon also writes in his paper "Truth about Punjab - SGPC White Paper":

"Santa Singh defied the order of ex-communication and continued the job at the Golden Temple which was under the possession of the army and where free entry to the pilgrims, as noted above, was not allowed. In fact, the very question of a pilgrim going there could not arise since the place had become just a reminder of a continuing tragedy and desecration. Santa Singh was paid Rupees one lac a day to keep himself and his men doing the allotted task assigned to him by the Government."

Dass would like to hear the opinions of the Sangat concerning the Nihangs.

Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh!

question: any sikh motorcyclists?
answer:
For sikh Motorcylist, there are only 2 thing to be considered and thats

1) The Law,

I used to ride a 400 CC sports bike in New Zealand , according to law there sikhs are permitted to ride uptil 50 Kms without a helmet, initially be ready to be stopped by lots of cops and do carry a copy of the LTSA page which has the Law about exemption, i used to even carry my school certificate as well along, to prove my religion to a few misguided cops, even then there were a series of letters to get the ticket waved.

After sometime the cops start getting used to seeing you on the bike and get more knowledgeable about the law, a minute thing compare to the pleasure of wearing your turban and riding the bike.

I have ridden uptil 130 kms PH without my turban coming off, though it depends how you tie your turban, and your riding position, i can say i hv seen plenty in india ride uptil 100 with their turbans on.

2) Safety Helmet/etc

Actually helmet gives a false sense of protection, atleast in the western countries where most bike accidents and deaths happen on speeds above 150 etc, at that speed on street roads even a helmet can't really save you, I sometimes wonder how many ppl would ride at that speed if they didnt hv helmets, most likely none and thought would presumable result in low accidents and deaths

I used to wear a helmet only when going on high speed rides, i had a XXL helmet , tie a patka and tie a thathi around my chin, so that my patka doesnt come off when removing the helmet, its also prohibited my beard from entangling with the helmet strap, and my jura isnt very big so that helps.

All and all, to keep enjoying the pleasure of riding always take Precaution and rely of road side awareness and make common sense your best safety measure, rest is risk that you need to take to enjoy some riding pleasure.

question: Does the word Anokha exists in Panjabi or Sanskrit?
answer:
[member] Ji,
I am replying for replying based on my a little knowledge so that some other members who know hindi/sanskrit/urdu more deeply can pick from there.
You know that meaning of most of the words depend upon the context they are used in.
Anokha is more a Punjabi and Hindi word which in some contexts mean Ajeev (hindi-urdu) or  unmatched/unparalleled/different/strange/uncommon/abnormal.
I think 'unique' literally does not mean Anokha but 'Anupam' (atulniya in pure hindi/uncomparable/beyond praise etc) which is also used for Anokha in some contexts.
In deep literal and liguistic meaning Anokha and Anupam(unique) are NOT 100% synonyms. I am sure of it.
In practice Anupam/Unique is always used for positive traits whereas Anokha can be used for negative ones as well.
Would  you like the name of your baby to be Anupam Singh with nickname Annu ?

question: Does the word Anokha exists in Panjabi or Sanskrit?
answer:
Waheguru ji ka khalsa
Waheguru ji ki fateh

Word 'Anokha' is a Punjabi word derived from Prakrit langauage. Prakrit was a version of Sanskrit spoken by ordinary people whereas Sanskrit was and still is a scholarly language. Word Anokha in Prakrit was pronounced as ਅਣੋਖਾ which means that which was not earlier seen with eyes ie unseen earlier hence unique. On the other hand Anupam, a Sanskrit word menas that is beyond praise ie whose good qualities are beyond description. The common people's version of Anupam is Anoop, a common name among Punjabis.

Guru Angad Dev ji's daughter was named  ਅਣੋਖੀ
Humbly

answer:

Amrit vela means prioritizing god in our life. If you can stay out late and still get up at spend time contemplating god, it is fine. But don’t use staying out late as a reason for not being able to prioritize god.

> I feel a sense dilemma when I try to follow the regime that ensures an Amrit Vela for me. question: few questions regarding beliefs
answer:
Thanks for being here on this site. Thanks for asking such beautiful questions. I do not know your age and grade so my answers will be general in nature.

> hey,
>
> I am a student and am looking for some answers that I have for an assignment, is there someone who can help me with my researech?
>
> Thanks!
>
> 1) What do you believe about God?
>
> 2) What do you believe about the universe?
>
> 3)What do you believe a out the nature of human beings?
>
> 4) how do you get knowledge?
>
> 5) How do you determine right and wrong?

1. There is one God, who has always existed and will continue to exist. Therefore, God is Truth - always existing. God is the creator, God resides in the creation, God is without fear and enmity, God is beyond time, never is born and therefore never dies, God is self created. God can only be reached by practising the way of life that a True Teacher guides you.

2. Universe is a manifestation of God. As God cannot be fathomed, so the universe that God created cannot be fathomed. God resides in the universe and is inseparable from the Universe.

3. Human beings are the creation of God. God resides in every human being. By nature, human being has an opportunity to realise God. Human beings are generally in a cycle of life and death. If a human being realises God, then that human being is freed from the cyle of life and death. While God has given a human being this unique gift of breaking away from cycle of life and death, God has also given some challenges. The five major chalenges are - a) ego, a feeling of separate entity from God, b) Anger, c) lust, d) Greed, and e) Attachment. Human being by nature stays engrossed in one, some or all of these challenges.

4. In sikh religion, one definition of God is knowledge. A sikh is expected to practise the religion rationally, diligently and intelligently. A sikh is  a seeker and student all life tme. In practise of religion, a sikh is expected to be literate to ponder over what the True Teacher teaches him and rationally follow it, earn living by working hard (not to beg or live on charity), lead ammried life, bring up children, meditate and share the earnings with others. A sikh is expected to be foresighted and alwys be ready to help others. This way, a sikh gathers knowledge about the surroundings, relationships, family, worldly affairs and spiritual life.

5. It is easy to determine right and wrong. In sikh religion, we believe that God resides inside you and your conscious constantly guides you as to what is right and wrong. When in doubt, just ask your own conscience. In a nut shell, any thought or action that takes you closer to God and strengthens your concience is right and the reverse of it is wrong. As a thumb rule, when you genuinely feel good from deep within you in doing something, that is right and go ahead and do it. As a religion, a sikh is asked to guard against some major wrong things - a) consuming drugs, alcohol, tobacco or similar intoxicants, b) not to harm/disturb/alter the human body of oneself, c) follow strict dietary habits, and d) consider everybody as your sibling, father or mother, depending on your age, other than your wedded partner.

Hope this is useful for your assignment.

question: Sikhs and turban
answer:
Waheguru ji ka khalsa
Waheguru ji ki fateh

I experienced this at the US Embassy in London 15 years ago for a US visa and Green Card. They wanted to have the photograph that shows the right ear so that the detailed folds of the ear could be used as a biometric identity. They suggested an Indian shop close by. They did not ask the turban to be retied or whatever. I simply lifted the edge of the last fold of my turban covering the right ear and had a passport sized photograph made. I didn't mind this security/identity precaution.

Different sikhs from different sampardas or sects tie their turbans differently and they are all sikhs. There is no particualr injunction from the Guru ji to tie a turban in a particular manner. In fact, there is no mention by Guru ji anywhere about the turban or how to tie it. The turban is a secular cultural item common to Indians, Pakistanis, mid-easterns. For Sikhs it is a necessity to keep the 'Kesh' covered, 'Kesh' being one of the identity stamps (mohar) from Guru ji but turban is just incidental artifact not anything sacrosanct or sacred about it. In young age, many urban sikh children use a 'Patka' and not the turban to cover their hair and women till recently never wore a turban and covered and still cover their kesh with a piece of cloth or Chunni.

Humbly

answer:

If the solution is only to tie your hair back in a ponytail/bun... I don't see the point because I assume you'll be wearing a turban once in the country anyway.

answer:
Certainly Not. These people are no where a gurikh. Whole me life i have been watching various understanding and definations of a sikh. As per my believe, a gursikh is a person who first of all believes in sewa (help), sacrifice (upliftment of other people) and helping others keeping his own interest aside. The duty of a sikh is to always raise voice to any injustice to others. He is also supposed to thanks god for everything he has got in his life, for every good or bad things happening in is life, in short he should always accept whatever he has got in his life and should never complain. He should always remeber god ie his mind should always be in the remembrence of god. Sikh literally means 'Student' or a person who wants to learn the path of rightouness. Now the path to rightouness is described in our religious books.All the religoius books, whether its Guru Granth Sahib, Gita, etc, are pointing towards this path may be through different routes. If you see even in Hindu religion people dont cut their hairs, dont drink or eat non veg during Navratras. That shows that even the hindu religion does not want you to cut your hairs or drink or eat. Its just that we human beings mold the things and make our own definations and own paths. some times you might have seen 2 different hindu families following  different rituals.
I believe, that one should not just read japji sahib or other banis, they should also try to understand what  each word means and then follow that path with his own understanding.

answer:
Definitely !

Doing such things is clearly a mockery of Sikh principles.

The very Baani of which paath is undertaken, says that mere oration of anything is not going to yield any good.

Gaaviye, Suniye, Mann rakhiye Bhaao
[Chant, Listen with Love in the heart.]

It is like reverting to ritualistic Hindu practices which Guru Sahib had vociferously condemned.

But I dont know how it could be stopped. It needs individual initiative. Or maybe directive from Akaal Takhat.

Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh

question: Akhandpaath in absentia be disallowed.
answer:
My own marriage had the customary sehaj paath prior to the actual day.  Our granthi was a young man with a young family and was in another city attending to the gurdwara there at the time.  My dadaji was very keen on this young man to perform the sehaj paath for us as he knew he would do it with love and best wishes for us, instead of the local gurdwara where some where strangers and unfortunately some may just be going through the paces.  (Yup that happens too).  This young granthi looked up to dadaji and was very mindful fo him.  He conducted the prayers with patience and affection.  He arrived in our city a couple of days prior to our wedding.  He continued with the paath and on the day finished the last section with my whole family in attendance and participating.  We all found his genuine nature, his genuine good wishes to myself and my hubby to be very moving and were deeply grateful he gave up his time from his family to do this for us.  In this instance I am glad in absentia was allowed.  If not we would have missed out on having such a wonderful person recite paath for us and conclude by conducting our anand karaj for us too.  He knew through my dadaji that I dearly wanted a granthi to perform our anand karaj and the bonus was that he had a connection to our family.

I am sure there are many instances where individuals are far way or have no connection with their local sangat or granthi but the sangat or granthi from their hometown would be mean so much more as often they become part of the extended family.

question: taking amrit first time _ bujjer kurehit
answer:
The Guru through his bani tells us how to have truthful living. The Guru also forgives us of our 'sins', gives us the advice to follow the correct path now onward by showing us the same. Amrit Ceremony is in conformity of this doctrine of the gurbani. It shows us the truthful path to start our spiritual journey fresh without the burden of guilt of the past mistakes (sins) committed inadvertently or otherwise due to lack of knowedge of the right path.

Bujjer Kurhiats have ben identified in the Rehat maryada and one is advised not to commit them to continue to be a sikh and receive the grace of the Waheguru.

When you are receiving the gift of the Aamrit from the Panj Piyare for the first time all our earlier mistakes are forgiven and Guru takes us in his lap and promises to guide you on the righteous path and warn us from time to time if we are following the Nitnem and reading and understadning the gurbani, so normally one would be prevented from falling in the trap of the bajjer kurhaits. However, if for some reasons one were to commit the Kurhait, the Guru does not banish us to the hell of the repentence, guilt and depodency but promises to put us again on the right path if we would submit to the authority of the Panj Piyare, who after hearing our case would determine what would be our religious punishmnet (tankah), which invariably will be doing some sewa of the sangat ina Gurudwara for a specified period followed by an Ardaas, offering of Prasad of the specified value and readminstration of the Amrit.

Guru Fateh.

question: Question regarding life after death.
answer:
Hello [member] hope you are well.
Human life is just a stage in the upward march of the soul. The individual has got birth as a human being, after going through lower forms of life. Human life is the final stage in the soul’s progress to divinity. It is for us to make the most of this opportunity and thereby end our cycle of transmigration.

ਅਨਿਕ ਜਨਮ ਬਹੁ ਜੋਨੀ ਭ੍ਰਮਿਆ ਬਹੁਰਿ ਬਹੁਰਿ ਦੁਖੁ ਪਾਇਆ ॥
ਤੁਮਰੀ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਤੇ ਮਾਨੁਖ ਦੇਹ ਪਾਈ ਹੈ ਦੇਹੁ ਦਰਸੁ ਹਰਿ ਰਾਇਆ ॥੧॥
“Wandering around through countless incarnations, I endured pain and suffering in so many lives, over and over again. By Your Grace, I obtained this human body; grant me the Blessed Vision of Your Darshan, O Sovereign Lord King. ||1||”
(Ang 207)

Death means the destruction of the physical self. The ashes and bone dust mix with the elements. But the soul which leaves the body, awaits a new dwelling. Just as a person casts off worn-out garments and puts on other that are new, so the subtle soul casts off the worn-out body and dwells in a new form. If there were no continuance of the soul after death, how could it become perfect to merit union with the Almighty?

Sikhism believes in the immortality of the soul.

ਕਹੀ ਨ ਉਪਜੈ ਉਪਜੀ ਜਾਣੈ ਭਾਵ ਅਭਾਵ ਬਿਹੂਣਾ ॥
ਉਦੈ ਅਸਤ ਕੀ ਮਨ ਬੁਧਿ ਨਾਸੀ ਤਉ ਸਦਾ ਸਹਜਿ ਲਿਵ ਲੀਣਾ ॥੩॥
ਜਿਉ ਪ੍ਰਤਿਬਿੰਬੁ ਬਿੰਬ ਕਉ ਮਿਲੀ ਹੈ ਉਦਕ ਕੁੰਭੁ ਬਿਗਰਾਨਾ ॥
ਕਹੁ ਕਬੀਰ ਐਸਾ ਗੁਣ ਭ੍ਰਮੁ ਭਾਗਾ ਤਉ ਮਨੁ ਸੁੰਨਿ ਸਮਾਨਾਂ ॥੪॥੧॥
“The soul is never born, though man thinks it is born, it is free from birth and death. When man’s idea of birth and death departs then, he, ever remains absorbed in Lord’s love. As, when pitcher breaks, the reflection in the water, blends with the object, similarly, says Kabir, when through virtue doubt flees, then, the soul is absorbed in the Profound Lord. ||4||1||”
(Ang 475)

The devotee has no fear of the pangs of death. In fact he welcomes death, because it gives him a chance for the merger into Divinity. The evil person, however, dreads death. For him, it will lead to the unending cycle of birth and death. After death, man comes to the next birth according to what he deserves. If he has been wicked and evil, he takes birth in the lower species. If he has done good deeds, he takes birth in a good family. The cycle of birth and death keeps the soul away from Divinity. It can merge with God, only if the individual, by spiritual effort, has amassed the capital of Naam, the Name of the Lord, and thus lives a life in the presence of the Divine.

In Sikhs the Holy Book "Granth Sahib" is considered as a "Guru", means the Holy Master (that's why Sikhs call their Holy Book, "Guru Granth sahib")

The First Chapter of this Book, "Japji Sahib" is considered as a key to the Book by many Sikhs...

ਗਾਵੈ ਕੋ ਸਾਜਿ ਕਰੇ ਤਨੁ ਖੇਹ ||

meaning: Some believe in 'the Re-birth' (like Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism) while others believe in 'the Last Day of Judgement' (like Muslims, Christians and Jews).

ਕਥਿ ਕਥਿ ਕਥੀ ਕੋਟੀ ਕੋਟਿ ਕੋਟਿ ||

meaning:  There is no limit for enumerating His Virtues. There is no dearth of millions,who sing Thy praise a million times.

ਨਾਨਕ ਵਿਗਸੈ ਵੇਪਰਵਾਹੁ ||

meaning: By His Command,our path has been chalked out, Leading us to blissful and peaceful life, says Nanak.

question: Reading SGGS in English
answer:
SSA,

Even though reading in English is good and the community is  eternally thankful to people who have spent time translating.
My personal opinion is that the meaning is quite often lost in translation (doesn't matter how good it is and how many times scholars have reviewed it).

Infact when i sometimes read SGGS in English available on Sikhnet (the translation is most popular available) , There are times i just cant stop thinking that the translation is just wrong. Apart from that a lot of  words don't have a exact word in English and many times we carry baggage with some words (usually forgetting the true meaning).

question: What paath to do for?
answer:
Here is an old Sikh tale & Shabad to contemplate -

All the learning in the world are of no use if we do not care to follow them

Setha, Gobinda and Bhaga were three rich merchants. They lived at Chaniot, a small town in Pakistan. All the three brothers were Hindus and the offered Sharadhs every year. They gave corn, clothes and coins to the Brahmans as Dakshana. Sometimes they wondered if all these things were really reached their forefathers in the next world.

One day they came to Guru Arjan Dev ji to find out his views about the Sharadhs and Dakshana. "O Guru," said Gobinda "We give Dakshana to the Brahmans in the name of our dear forefathers every year. Tell us whether all this reaches our forefathers or not?"

"No man can tell whether your forefathers are in heaven or hell." said the Guru smilingly. "No one can tell which Brahman will go to heaven and which to hell. Moreover even if a Brahman reaches your forefathers, how can he recognize them out of the millions of dead people? Stop thinking about such things and stop offering Sharadhs. Work hard, tell the truth, help others and remember God."

The three brothers agreed to act upon the Guru's advice and were satisfied, but there was another man, named Chuhar, who couldn't understand the Guru's advice. He said "Sir, how can a merchant like myself and people like Gobinda always speak the truth? Merchants have to tell many lies between sunrise and sunset every day."

“Go back to your village, Chuhar,” said the Guru. “Do your trading and try to act upon my advice. Everyday count your lies and good deeds, write them down on a piece of paper and show me that paper at the end of every month.” Chuhar agreed to act upon the Guru’s advice and went away.

From that day onwards. Chuhar counted and wrote down his lies and good deeds on a piece of paper. At the end of a month he came with it and showed it to the Guru The Guru asked him to read it out to the Sikhs and Chuhar did so. He had done no good deeds and had told a number of lies. He felt small and thought that he should have done better. The Guru however smiled and said, "Chuhar, leave your paper here and keep on trying."

At the end of the second month, Chuhar had really done some good deeds and had told fewer lies. And so it went on. At the end of the eighth month, Chuhar's lies and good deeds were added up. This showed that although he had done only a few good deeds, he had told no lies. Everybody was surprised. Guru Arjan Dev ji said, "All advice falls flat on those who never think of acting upon it. People have been listening to good advice for thousands of years. The important thing is to act upon it. Cart-loads of books and all the learning in the world are of no use if we do not care to follow them."

All the Sikhs understood the Guru's advice and promised to act upon it.

Shabad
http://searchgurbani.com/scriptures/ggs_shabad/500/line/5

This Gurdwara was one of the five forts constructed by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur Sahib for the defense of the Sikhs. Guru Gobind Singh spent 25 years at Anandpur Sahib. To protect the Sikhs from the hill Rajas or Mughals, Guru Gobind Singh began the construction of five defensive forts all around the town. Keshgarh at the center (now a Takht), Anandgarh (fort of bliss), Lohgarh (fort of steel), Holgarh (fort of colour) and Fatehgarh (fort of victory). All the forts were joined together with earthworks and underground tunnels. The construction began in 1689 and took over ten years to complete.

question: Sikh Studies Question
answer:
Veerji,

I encourage you to do what your heart/mind desires.  Granted, there may not be job security as there is in engineering, especially if you stay in India.  However, I think that if you truly love what you study, and choose to make a career out of teaching and learning about Sikhi, and keep faith in Babaji's plan, it should be less scary.

There is an excellent Sikh Studies program here in the U.S.:

[link]

Years ago, I asked the same question that you did, on this very same discussion board.  And a very kind soul referred me to my now-adviser, Professor Gurinder Singh Mann.  He is an incredibly kind man and has dedicated his life to the field.  The students here at [place] love and respect him dearly.  While other scholars would take summers off, Professor Mann has used every summer of the last twelve years, to take students to Punjab, and to develop their curiosity of the religions, history, and general landscape of Punjab.  I am so grateful to the community here; if it wasn't for them, I wouldn't be where I am now.

If you can't do it right now -- which is understandable -- you can always pursue academic studies (in the U.S.) when it is more feasible for you.  There are many people who attend graduate school (i.e. M.A. level and up) after having had a career in another field altogether, raising families, et cetera.  So, don't feel discouraged -- your options are still open!

extra.question_body: Sat sri akal friends, please share what is the meaning of AJAPPA  JAAP.

question: a query
answer:
[member],

Initially naam jaap requires effort.  Our mind wanders and the exercise feels like an uninteresting chore.  The Guru advises us to continue this effort even if we don't like it.
ਕਰਹਿ  ਜਿ  ਗੁਰ  ਫੁਰਮਾਇਆ  ਸਿਲ  ਜੋਗੁ  ਅਲੂਣੀ  ਚਟੀਐ  ॥  He does as the Guru commands; He tasted the tasteless stone (SGGS 966)

If we continue, with Guru's grace, there comes a stage when the naam jaap continues uninterrupted without any effort this is called ajaapa jaap.

When a tuner tunes a musical instrument he strikes a tuning fork and holds the stem of the fork next to the instrument.  Then he adjusts the instrument and suddenly sound comes out of the instrument automatically as soon as the frequency of the instrument matches that of the tuning fork. Naam is similar.  Our ego has pushed the frequency of our mind out of step from God.  Naam simran slowly removes our ego, and our mind starts purifying and starts moving closer to the frequency of God.  Initially we have to work hard on simran, after some time our mind comes in resonance with God, then the simran continues effortlessly and become ajaapa jaap.  At this stage:
-  A Gurmukh is able to hear anhad naad, the celestial music that plays in cosmos all the time.
- There is naam in everything and everyplace.  The gurmukh becomes a part of naam, and 'rom rom' simran (simran from every pore of body) begins.
-  What a gurmukh says comes true.  Bhai Vir Singh ji pointed out that people sometimes confuse these actions as miracles.  When in fact the gurmukh is not changing/affecting God's hukam, but his/her mind being in resonance with hukam just vocalizes, in sehaj, what's about to happen.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

answer:
As per the link provided by the moderator, which appears to be another well studied and scholarly answer by [member], we need to consider the greater picture furthermore.

Furthermore, whatever the Guru's Willed they could make happen in the world, but as is seen by the Katha's of 9th Guru, in his humility he would always forgive (even after being shot at) and allow God's will to prevail.

Furthermore, the Guru's in their wisdom did not need to 'control' or make the world change for them, as per Divine Wisdom they would accept that all is God's creation. They realized that the false will exist, and for all time challenge the resolve of Sikhs.

Furthermore, as there is evidence upon the false Sikhs from the very beginning, the various false and self proclaiming Guru's. We see that many are takers and susceptible to the mind being their master. There will come a time as prophesied that the false Khalsa will be washed away, and the Lotus of True Khalsa will blossom in all places.

Furthermore, we must take upon this the message that we must go and follow the Guru. Not any place, not any attachments of the mind. There are always lessons to be learned.

Furthermore, we must go inward, realise our inner conscious, take the path to self realisation, and continue to ascribe to the Guru's Will. We must invoke this and release ourselves of the bondage of the mind.

answer:
There are 4 main rules that must not be broken and if they are then you MUST go to the Panj Pyare.
1. Must not eat meat
2. mustn't take alcohol /drugs
3. must not cut hair
4. must not have affair outside marriage.

Other than that we are all going to make errors/mistakes. As suggested by first poster

Agreed,this is not neccessary.
With regards to "Sikh should do kirpan bheta and say ardas and then it is not halal". The reason for doing "bhog" on langar is not to make it non-halal, it is as an offering to God who then "consumes" it.

question: becoming a sikh
answer:
Hello brother Greetings,
It's a matter of great delight to know that you have found Sikhi as the path to Spirituality.Nice that it's making sense to you.

Let me tell you the basics of Sikhism, Firstly it never believes in leading an aesthetic life, it's all about living in this World doing your deeds in a righteous manner and reciting the name of God. Secondly, though the concept of God is monotheistic but it's way different than the concept of Abrahamic God, we call it as ultimate Reality which contains everything in it, it's all powerful stable ONE who resides in everyone's heart and each human soul needs to perfect itself so that it can finally attain it's ultimate goal of reaching it's permanent Home that is merging with Lord God. Every thing in this creation is contained within God, Much like saying "as Above, so Below" With these concepts in mind you must proceed ahead with a stable mind and heart towards Sikhism. So Welcome!!!!!!!!!!!!

Now the question comes of your becoming a Sikh. In concept Sikhism never see any faith superior or inferior to anyone. It just emphasizes that each individual needs to connect to the true Name of the God irrespective of the faith in which they are born into. This is what our tenth Sikh Master Guru Gobind Singh writes:-

IIThe Yogis perform Yoga, many are absorbed in doing Pranayama and residents of Arabia remember Thy Name.II
IIThe people of France revere Thee, the inhabitants of Kandhaar and Quraishis know Thee; the people of western side recognize their duty towards Thee.II
.
.
.
II Those who meditated on Thee, they obtained perfect Glory (identification with God) they prosper greatly with wealth, fruit and flowers in their homes.II (Earthly & Spiritual Homes)

Hence it's all about Meditating and craving for True Name, for that you must have hunger for obtaining true name. If you are ready for it and have the urge inside you then Sikhism is for you. You don't need to go to the Hills and meditate, neither you need to perform postures of Yoga.. Just need to have true longing for Lord, in Sikhism u remember him sing his praises through Sikh prayers as it is accurate in that sense because it(Sikh prayers) eulogises the glory of that Almighty Lord.

And if you have sincere longing in this direction and want to adopt the Sikh Culture externally too you can visit a Gurudwra (Sikh Worshipping place) and consult the priests and people attached with Gurdwara.
Hope this provides some answer to your queries, for further queries you are free to ask any question that arise in your heart mate.

question: pomp & show
answer:
[member],
The kind of celebration described in your post are social in nature and not as per the gurmat.

Each family wants to use the ocassion of marriage of their offspring to show to the 'world' that they have 'arrived' and they are able to keep up with the Jonesses or being one up on them so they indulge in all kind of splurge including very elaborate decoarations, entertainment and meals. Some of the families can really affoard it and are only giving business to the new industry of wedding event managers but the problem is for those who can not affoard but are forced by 'social demands/ pressure' to undertake such arrangements at huge costs to them which may affect their finances for the rest of their lives. I have understood that young people who are getting married demand of their parents that such 'nice' wedding ceremonies be organized for them so that they can feel that they belong to the class they think they belong.

Let us start to overcome these issues by starting from our homes. Have a simple wedding at gurdwara followed by a simple meal and no more ceremonies and entertainment. May be some others will follow you.

Guru fateh.

[member]

question: Quotes of gurbani on daughters/girls
answer:
ਮਃ ੧ ॥
मः १ ॥
Mėhlā 1.
First Mehl:

ਭੰਡਿ ਜੰਮੀਐ ਭੰਡਿ ਨਿੰਮੀਐ ਭੰਡਿ ਮੰਗਣੁ ਵੀਆਹੁ ॥
भंडि जमीऐ भंडि निमीऐ भंडि मंगणु वीआहु ॥
Bẖand jammī▫ai bẖand nimmī▫ai bẖand mangaṇ vī▫āhu.
From woman, man is born; within woman, man is conceived; to woman he is engaged and married.

ਭੰਡਹੁ ਹੋਵੈ ਦੋਸਤੀ ਭੰਡਹੁ ਚਲੈ ਰਾਹੁ ॥
भंडहु होवै दोसती भंडहु चलै राहु ॥
Bẖandahu hovai ḏosṯī bẖandahu cẖalai rāhu.
Woman becomes his friend; through woman, the future generations come.

ਭੰਡੁ ਮੁਆ ਭੰਡੁ ਭਾਲੀਐ ਭੰਡਿ ਹੋਵੈ ਬੰਧਾਨੁ ॥
भंडु मुआ भंडु भालीऐ भंडि होवै बंधानु ॥
Bẖand mu▫ā bẖand bẖālī▫ai bẖand hovai banḏẖān.
When his woman dies, he seeks another woman; to woman he is bound.

ਸੋ ਕਿਉ ਮੰਦਾ ਆਖੀਐ ਜਿਤੁ ਜੰਮਹਿ ਰਾਜਾਨ ॥
सो किउ मंदा आखीऐ जितु जमहि राजान ॥
So ki▫o manḏā ākẖī▫ai jiṯ jamėh rājān.
So why call her bad? From her, kings are born.

ਭੰਡਹੁ ਹੀ ਭੰਡੁ ਊਪਜੈ ਭੰਡੈ ਬਾਝੁ ਨ ਕੋਇ ॥
भंडहु ही भंडु ऊपजै भंडै बाझु न कोइ ॥
Bẖandahu hī bẖand ūpjai bẖandai bājẖ na ko▫e.
From woman, woman is born; without woman, there would be no one at all.

ਨਾਨਕ ਭੰਡੈ ਬਾਹਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਸਚਾ ਸੋਇ ॥
नानक भंडै बाहरा एको सचा सोइ ॥
Nānak bẖandai bāhrā eko sacẖā so▫e.
O Nanak, only the True Lord is without a woman.

ਫਰੀਦਾ ਬੁਰੇ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ ਕਰਿ ਗੁਸਾ ਮਨਿ ਨ ਹਢਾਇ ॥
Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.
ਦੇਹੀ ਰੋਗੁ ਨ ਲਗਈ ਪਲੈ ਸਭੁ ਕਿਛੁ ਪਾਇ ॥੭੮॥

These shabads are not for boys or girls. These are for everyone. So put it in every room. Read every day to implement in your life. (If you hang these quotes on wall as show piece then it has no value. Its beauty comes out when it becomes part of your family life)

Best age to teach kids when they are below 10 years old. Do Japji Sahib with them in morning and At night bed time start with simran (with Waheguru and Mool mantar Jaap) then Anand sahib 6 pauri then kirtan sohila. Discuss meaning of gurbani and listen kids stories with them on sikhnet media app.

Ask them to do mool mantar every time before eating and say thanks to waheguru when they get or done something.

Become role model for them. Fill them with gurbani teachings. This is best gift you can give to them. Without naam the world is burning. Whoever has support of Naam these fires cannot touch them.

Kids Stories: http://www.sikhnet.com/stories

Thanks!

question: A Gurmukh needs an advise
answer:
It should not be taken as generalization but I have found most of the sewadars in Gurdwaras in India the type one you have mentioned in your post.I have rarely come across a soft-spoken or polite sewadar in Indian Gurdwaras. This could be because of stress of kind of work they use to do or lack of understanding of their duty and religion.Their behavior towards non-sikhs and trimmed-beard Sikhs is quite discriminatory. They behave like special custodians of religion or that of shrines.I strongly believe that they need hospitality kind of education/training and also proper understanding of their role and duty as Sikhs.
I have not been to any Gurdwara in western countries except in UK and have found those people well mannered than their counterparts in India.
As of your case in US, I can understand that it is easier said than done to tell some one to 'forget the insult meted out to you'. You should at least report this matter to mgmt of that Gurdwara or any other Sikh social/cultural organisations of that place. People of typical Indian/Punjabi mentality use to look down at 'new-comers', be it place of work or worship and do not miss any opportunity to vent out their own frustrations caused by the situations they had faced when they were new-comers. In some cases they also look at new comers as potential threat to their 'position'.

question: Taming the Beard
answer:
Hmm... it is very difficult to visualize exactly what you are saying.

However, know that your beard will for the most part set itself. And initially you will be worried about how it looks, because it needs some length before its striking image will remind you of the various Sikhs who gave their lives in sacrifice for the freedom that we enjoy today. When you adopt such a path with such volition, your mind will begin to think in a different way. To most in the world the beard is unappealing, but to you you will be in awe.
Do not get me wrong, this is not a egoistic awe. This is an awe of the nature of the world. We live in a world where much nature is destroyed. One wonders if the humans have destroyed so much of nature when will it take its revenge? It appears the hurricanes, tornadoes, floods (even in US, UK and like) are the message from nature ("you have forsaken me").

Besides the point, here are some tips. Use an oil to comb the beard twice daily with. You will have to find one that suits you. Amla oil is quite popular, most oils are scented in some way. Additionally at the outset the beard is likely going to grow out to the sides at equal length to the bottom. Do not fear, the nature of the beard is that it will grow longer at the chin than out to the side. You have to trust that this will happen in time. As you change and keep looking in the mirror, you may become overly focused in your 'looks'. The point you stop caring is the point that you have overcome your egoic self (not entirely, but that aspect of it).

extra.question_body: I have been growing out my hair and beard, but since I have very curly hair, my beard has been getting larger in volume more than longer in length. What are some tips for keeping the beard looking neat and in check without cutting it? I have heard of both compressing it with gel and tying it, but I don't really know how to efficiently go about either. Please offer any and all advice/technique/brands to use etc.

question: Taming the Beard
answer:
Dear Spiritual Seeker, Sat Sri Akal!

Congratulations on growing your beard and respecting God's manly gift to us males which is to be cherished and preserved as best as we can.A Sikh is obliged to look smart and well turned out without interfering with the natural aspect of his body within sensible and human constraints.Many Sikhs adopt the British-originated practice of fixing,pasting,threading,curling the beard,etc as some of the many ways of making it "neat and tidy".They tried to make us 'gentlemen'!But I am personally against this as Guru has asked us to adorn a full-flowing beard(lion's mane) redardless of how self-conscious we may feel about it.It soon becomes second nature.

Use a brush as well as your Kangha( one of the 5 K's,a wooden comb tucked in your hair behind your top-knot)as often as you can.The more you groom your beard lovingly,the more "tame" it gets.But for heavens sake,do not ever get so irritated as to think of trimming or cutting,as that will be retrogressive and a big step backwards,which you don't ever want to do.Be loving to yourself,to Guru's gift and to Nature,and ultimately to God Almighty whose faithful children we aspire to be.

So best wishes and good beard-management!

question: Sikh blessing for weddings and other important life events?
answer:
[member],

I hope I am not responding to your query too late after the event has already passed.  First of all, congratulations and best wishes for your upcoming wedding.

Indian community has a wide variety of rituals and ceremonies, from your description its hard for me to identify what this particular ceremony is.  However, based on your clue that this reading is done for weddings and other important life events, I think that the reading may be of "Anand Sahib".  Anand means bliss, and Sahib is a term of respect.  Anand Sahib is a poetic compilation of 40 stanzas in Punjabi, and was introduced by the Third Guru.  Its customary to sing six stanzas (first five and the last stanza), and sometimes all 40 stanzas are sung.  Anand Sahib is sung on all important life events including birth, wedding and death.

Anand Sahib has been one of my favorite readings from very young age.  The language is easy to understand, the compilation is very melodic, and it covers many different aspects of Sikhism.  You can read Anand Sahib and its English translation at the link below:
http://www.srigranth.org/servlet/gurbani.gurbani?Action=Page&Param=917&g=1&h=1&r=1&t=1&p=0&k=0&fb=0

If the blessing event is still in the future, please try to find out which gurbani will be read, and members on this forum will be able to provide you more background.  Please share your experience with us.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Sikhism - the future
answer:
[member] ji,

I do agree with your suggestions 1 to 4. I realise that a lot of thing are done in this field already my main critique on all this is that although the intentions are right and the effort is great the result seems to be poor. I think most of these promotional actions lack a clear vision on which groups to target and what goals are to be reached. I think people should take a step back and think about these subjects before diving into promotional activities.

On your point 5 I'm not that sure anymore. When I first found Sikhism (just 3 months ago) I thought "off course SGGS should be translated to every language in the world. People need to be able to acces it". I still think everybody should be able to acces SGGS. But translating the Sikh Rehat Maryada I changed my mind about translations. The main reason being that translations may gradually shift the meaning of what is written. So translation is a real dilemma. On the one hand I would say yes on the other hand I would say no.
As a matter of fact I think the translation of the Rehat Maryada would bring a new generation closer to Sikh way of life (I do not want to boost myself though) as it contains the Sikh code of conduct and conventions.

Perhaps a translation of the SGGS should only be just that and not be the SGGS itself (So the translation should not be the living Guru). The translation should only be the 'practical' door to the SGGS.

I was in a Gurdwara for the first time last weekend and listened to the reciting of Shukmani Sahib (well part of it at least). Not knowing any Gurmukti or Punjabi I couldn't understand what was recited I thought it would be great to have subtitling with it. (like on Dutch tv where foreign movies have the original speach but have also Dutch subtitles)

I do realise the impractiality/impossiblity of everybody learning Gurmukti.

extra.question_body:
Hello Friends,

I wished to engage like minded members in discussion around a very pertinent topic effecting each of our lives.

What is the future of Sikhism ?
Would Sikhism continue with its external symbols intact ?
How can the Sikh way of living be promoted amongst the youth and next generations ?

I find many families struggling to push their next generation in being SIKHS (looks). Parents push children without any proper justification and end up disputing the young generations views on this topic.

I have some suggestions -

1. Sikhs should promote more role models who practice Sikhism. Today, Sikhs are remembered more as warriors and happy go lucky people everywhere. We need to push more role models from other fields like management, economy, doctors, other professionals which can really boost image of Sikhism amongs the youth. Remember, these are the career most of the youth are looking forward to and would really boost their self esteem.

2. We should promote through new media and other mediums some of the practical importance of being Sikhs in the today's world. e.g. There are no beggars in Sikh community. This is a great achievement in today's context of economical divide. I think this is a matter of pride for most Sikhs. We need to make people understand on why is so ? Our community bonding principles of 'Kirt Karo, Naam Japo, Wand SHako' really make sense to today's world.

3. I have worked in many countries like Singapore, Malaysia, UK and India ( I work with [place] now). I can say with pride that my turban and external appearance have always helped me in breaking the ice. I have never faced any discrimination in any of these countries which may have impacted my career. Contrarily, a lot of people come to me out of curiousity and when they understand on why we have this appearance, our history, our pride in what we are, they respect you as a person. We should promote more such experiences.

4. Sikhism is one of the most practical and modern religions. We need to promote why in today's context to the youth. We had one of the most secular history (our highest shrine's foundation stone was laid down by a Muslim), we had the equal status for women for centuries, Sikh's believe in current life - what we sow in this life would reap results in the same life....we really need to promote these principles.

5. This is my personal view - I feel that Sri Guru Granth Sahib should be translated into common man's language. Let it start from Daily Hukumnama...we know the real meaning of Hukumnama which can be a translation...but it's interpretation in today's life should also be highlighted. I know it is tough job but would really bring the new generation closer to Sikh way of life.

I would love some active discussion on the topic.

Cheers,

[member]

question: How to commit yourself to do something?
answer: Hello again (I believe that we have met on another discussion).  I agree with you very much.  It is proven that human nature commits moreso when it is interesting and (sadly) when there is something of self gain (or 'in-it-for-me').  I am not, at all, suggesting that this applies to you but something to think about.  I think, that as a Sikh, it is our duty to abandon this selfish act and think more broadly (I refer - and not so well - to the ideology of caring for our wider society).  Maybe you need to think about what it is that you want to give to society and pursue your career in that way.  I dont think that anyone can give us an answer to 'how to commit' as it is such a personal thing.  Just remember that no matter what it is that you do, it will have a lasting effect on both you and your surrounding (human and nonhuman).  Isn't that an amazing concept in itself - and certainly one to encourage commitment?  Best of luck!!!

Approximate composition per 100g

question: ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰੀਓ inflected form?
answer:
Hi [member],

You have misspelled the word 'Kareo', the correct spelling is: ਕਰਿਓ.  May be that's why you couldn't find the phrase in your Punjabi Kosh.

I can think of the following usages of the two forms:
•	Both can be used in present tense verb.  As in “Forgive me” "ਮੈਨੂੰ ਮਾਫ ਕਰਨਾ", or "ਮੈਨੂੰ ਮਾਫ ਕਰਿਓ".
•	Only "ਮਾਫ ਕਰਿਓ" can be used in a past tense.  As in "God forgave sinners, and then set them on the right path".  "ਪ੍ਰਮਾਤਮਾ ਨੇ ਪਾਪੀਆਂ ਨੂੰ ਮਾਫ ਕਰਿਓ ਤੇ ਸਿਧੇ ਰਸਤੇ ਪਾਇਓ".  However, this type of usage is rare.
•	Only "ਮਾਫ ਕਰਨਾ" can be used as a noun.  As in: "Act of forgiving somebody is a good thing" "ਕਿਸੇ ਨੂੰ ਮਾਫ ਕਰਨਾ ਚੰਗੀ ਗੱਲ ਹੈ".  I can't think of any way to use ਮਾਫ ਕਰਿਓ as a noun.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰੀਓ inflected form?
answer:
[member] Ji, thanks for reply. Replies like yours with the correct spelling and examples of the words in a sentence help a lot.

The reason I was spelling it ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰੀਓ instead of ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਿਓ was because I was spelling the word from Shahmukhi (I read and write in Shahmukhi). The Shahmukhi spelling is ماف کريو which indicates it is spelled with a ਿਬਹਾਰੀ. However, the Gurmukhi spelling (most popular spelling) has a ਿਸਹਾਰੀ like this => ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਿਓ. I see this a lot between Shahmukhi and Gurmukhi words.

Demonstrated below...
ماف کريو = ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰੀਓ
ماف كِرو = ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਿਓ

I still have questions pertaing to ਕਰਿਓ though.
First, ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ is much easier to understand. ਮਾਫ਼ is an adjective meaning "excused, pardoned, etc.". ਕਰਨਾ is a verb meaning "to do". Together, the 2 words form a verb phrase meaning "to excuse, to pardon, etc.". This is easy to understand.

Okay, so now I have the verb phrase ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਿਓ. It means "to ask to excuse, to ask to pardon, etc.". This also makes sense as this would explain why it is considered more polite (than ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ). ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ is telling someone to excuse you, pardon you, etc.. Whereas, ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਿਓ is asking someone to excuse you, pardon you, etc..

This brings me to the heart of my question. Since ਕਰਨਾ means "to do", then how does ਕਰਿਓ mean "to ask to do"? Unless ਕਰਿਓ is a variation of ਕਰੋ? This would make perfect sense if it did. This would explain the difference in meaning.

extra.question_body:
Is "ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰੀਓ" and inflected form of "ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ"?

"ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ" is listed in my ਪੰਜਾਬੀ kosh as a verb meaning to pardon, to excuse, etc..

I am not able to find "ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰੀਓ". So, is "ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰੀਓ" an inflected form of "ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ"?

If it is, how is student of ਪੰਜਾਬੀ supposed to know this information? Where can I find this information?

question: ਭਾਸ਼ਾ ਬੋਲੀ ਜ਼ਬਾਨ
answer:
No word earlier existed to denote dialects. People would simply say the so and so speaks the language of Doabias, or that of Malwaees or that of Majhails to explain the spoken language of the Doaba, Malwa, or Majha region. However, the scholars of Panjabi language have borrowed a cue from Hindi linguists, ie 'ਉਪਬੋਲੀ' in Panjabi  pronounced as Upboli meaning a sub-language. Hindi scholars use the word Upbhasha for dialect.

question: Paath while working
answer:
The mind will wander as it is something we have asked our mind to do since birth. Getting it to occupy in something or other. It can be like playing, reading, socialising, movies, chats, etc. When one is tired of one thing a person moves to another activity saying - I am so bored. You will not see this in animals. You will see a cow, dog, or even a donkey sitting silently when it has eaten. They will just sit with eyes closed because their mind is not restless as ours.
The babaji you talked to gave the right advice of doing seva. Seva is physical activity in name og god. It has to be selfless. As per the physical strength one can do any seva. Washing, cleaning cooking, etc. It can be even done at home. One just needs to think that whatever he/she is doing is in service to god. This is the best way to keep your mind busy. Instead it will wander here and there. Whenever one doesn't feels like sitting in simran and gurbani reading, one should start doing seva immediately.
Both seva and simran have same outcome -
BHARIYE MATT PAPA KE SANG OH DHOPE NAAVE KE RANG
KOT PARADH MITHE HAR SEVA.

Both clean the mind and slowly over time mind settles.

Even if one doesn't absorbs mind in gurbani , one should make effort to continue doing it.
Guru says - GURBANI SUNN MAIL GAVAYE... Even if you don't understand it, it keeps cleaning your mind... You will see the results overtime.
I would ask you not to do paath till 20 pauri as it is incomplete. Instead do PAATH of 1st pauri till NANAK HOSI BHI SACH when you are working or moving around. It will benefit you more...

question: Paath while working
answer:
Benji
All reciting of bani is good. If you just know the mantra Waheguru, then just repeat Waheguru, Waheguru, waheguru. If you know just Ekh-oan-kaar, then just repeat this. If you just know Mool Mantra, then just repeat this. If you know 20 pauries of Japji Sahib then repeat this. Most people say they will do simran but never get round to it so just start, Guru Ji will do the rest.

Sometimes repeating 20 pauries or full japji Sahib may not be possible as you may get distracted at work or someone comes to talk to you etc, it may be that it is better just to repeat Mool Mantra, but if you can do 20 pauries then that is also good.

If you want to meet Guru Gobind Singh Ji  then try repetition of Chaupai Sahib from beginning of Akaal Ustat – Pranvo Aadh Ekonkaara…. Quite short chaupai and easy to  learn, this is good to repeat in your mind.

Have you noticed that your mind never wonders when you are watching a movie? Or reading a magazine or book? But  your mind will wonder every time you try to do something that moves you towards your Guru. This is because those five within you get very active when you start to do paath or simran. So be aware of them, know what is going on in your mind. But don’t be disheartened as this battle will rage for as long as you are doing simran, it only  gets easier by Gurparsad, Guru Ji’s kirpa.

Seva is when you do selfless service to your Guru. Remember Guru Ji resides in the sangat so if you do service of the sangat you are doing seva of your Guru. So go to the gurdwara and do any work, wash dishes, wash pots and pans, clean out the toilets. Help in the langar, clean the tables. Clean the tiolets?” this is your ego speaking, ignore it and do the seva, slowly nimarta will enter your mind because without nimarta/humbleness you cannot ever meet your Guru. question: Difference between 'Gossip' and 'discussion' in Sikhism
answer:
Brother [member],

You may be confusing "Slander" with "Gossip".  Gossip is not a good thing, but I don't believe its something specifically prohibited/discouraged in Sikhism.  Slander, on the other hand, is thoroughly discouraged in Sikhism.

In Sikhism, any time spent without remembrance of God is considered wasted time, its equated to sleep or death.  Using this definition, gossip (idle chit chat) would be a waste of valuable time.  It will be rare to find somebody whose every moment is spent in remembrance.  Sikhism is a journey, for most of us, the target is to maximize our time in remembrance.  If we are wasting time in other pursuits, we are not necessarily bad people, we are simply not being the best we can be.  If the chit chat is innocuous then its no worse than watching TV.  If chit-chat is being used to gloat or put somebody down, or to draw pleasure at somebody's expense, then it would be harmful to one's soul.  As I have just done, one may be able to find indirect references within SGGS to show that gossip is not good.  However, off hand I cannot think of any direct references in SGGS where gossip may be discouraged or prohibited.

Slander on the other hand is expressly discouraged in many places within SGGS.  Slander by definition is knowingly using false or questionable information to harm or put somebody down.  There are no restrictions on discussion or criticism in Sikhism, specially if its constructive.

Waheguru ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Identity Crisis
answer:
[member] ji,

We are social beings and our need to belong to a particular group is important to us.  Therefore, I can understand your dilemma.  However, the true Sikhism is more than just external appearances or our family/group affiliations.  The true Sikhism grows inside us and it's defined by how effectively we learn from the Guru.  My suggestion to you is to continue learning from the Guru without paying much attention to the Hindu/Sikh labels.

Guru Nanak Dev ji met Shah Saraf while walking from Jeddah to Mecca, and their dialog available in old manuscripts is known as 'Meccay Medina di Gost'.  According to this document (Twarikh Guru Khalsa, Volume 1, p 180), the Guru says, "Listen O Shah Saraf.  First the fakiri has to grow inside - just like the essence of a fruit which grows inside the tree before it becomes visible outside".  I think Sikhi is no different than fakiri, continue working on growing it inside you, when the time is right with the Guru's grace the external manifestations will follow.

The following is an excerpt from the translated autobiography of Sant Syed Prithipal Singh, where he describes Sikhism:

Sikhism is not what most people think it is.  A Sikh is: “ਆਪਿ ਜਪੈ ਅਵਰਾ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਾਏ ॥ The One who himself chants the Naam, and inspires others to chant it as well – SGGS 140.”  The meaning of Sikhism is not religion.  The moment we think that Sikhism means religion, we go against Gurbani, and we insult the Formless God.  The Guru explains what Sikhism is: “ਸਿਖੀ ਸਿਖਿਆ ਗੁਰ ਵੀਚਾਰਿ ॥ ਨਦਰੀ ਕਰਮਿ ਲਘਾਏ ਪਾਰਿ ॥ [The one who learns] the lesson through contemplating on the Guru.  [the merciful God’s] grace ferries that person across – SGGS 465”.  The following three requirements are fundamental for a Sikh: 1) Reading Gurbani,  2) Contemplating Gurbani, and 3) Following Gurbani.  If somebody meets these three requirements, then that person can thump his or her chest and claim: I am a Sikh, Nanak is mine, and I am Nanak’s.  It’s useless pride If somebody claims that they are Sikh because they were born in a Sikh household.  This pride will lead to a disaster: “ਪਉੜੀ ਛੁੜਕੀ ਫਿਰਿ ਹਾਥਿ ਨ ਆਵੈ ਅਹਿਲਾ ਜਨਮੁ ਗਵਾਇਆ ॥ Once slipped from a ladder its hard to regain a hold, that person’s life is wasted uselessly and this opportunity will not come back – SGGS 796.”  You will get to Guru’s house only if you follow the objectives of Sikhism.  Sikhism is to realize: “ਮਨ ਤੂੰ ਜੋਤਿ ਸਰੂਪੁ ਹੈ ਆਪਣਾ ਮੂਲੁ ਪਛਾਣੁ ॥ O my mind, you are embodiment of the divine light, recognize your true origin – SGGS – 441”.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh
