question: Types of Prayer
answer: bow down in respect. ask for guidance and be thankful

extra.question_body:
Hello everyone. :)
I'm currently exploring my Spirituality and seeking to find my own truth, and my current focus is in Islam and Sikhism.
I absolutely love the principles of Sikhism, the concept of Divinity, and the broad range of beliefs within it.

I suppose I will ask many more questions in the future, but for now I have a question concerning prayer.

Within the Abrahamic faiths (Judaism, Christianity, and Islam), prayer can be something prescriptive (such as the five daily prayers within Islam, or the Lord's Prayer within Christianity)

Also in these religious paths, prayer can simply be communicating with the Divine; expressing gratitude, asking for guidance, sharing your burdens, etc.

My question is about the latter;
In Sikhism, is it acceptable or traditional to simply talk to God? As opposed to complex ritualistic prescribed prayers, may I simply bow my head, ask for guidance, express gratitude, etc.? Or do Sikhs believe prayer to simply be a meditative state of stripping the ego and connecting to Divinity? Do Sikhs believe that God has a personal relationships with humans?

It seems to me that in many Eastern religions, this type of informal and direct prayer isn't as common as mantras and meditative prayers. But I personally tend to feel my most Spiritually connected when I can simply address God and be in communication.

Can anyone guide me?
Thank you.

question: Types of Prayer
answer:
Hi [member],

Congratulations for exploring spirituality - both Islam and Sikhism are wonderful paths.  You are correct in believing that prayers in Sikhism are a conversation with God and do not involve formality or rituals.  However, the Guru has asked us to recite Gurbani on a daily basis as form of a prayer.  This is not a ritual, as Gurbani is also a conversation with God (in the form of praise, supplication and gratitude).  In addition, the Gurbani reminds us to continue conversing with God at all times and it also provides us guidance on what type of conversation would benefit us the most.

There is a joke in Punjabi about prayers.  There lived a devout farmer in a village who spent most of his time conversing with God.  His next door neighbor was a potter who owned a donkey.  One day suddenly a problem arose.  Every time the farmer was in the middle of milking his cow, the neighbor's donkey would bray loudly and startle the cow which would jump and spill the milk.  The farmer talked to the neighbor and tried all sorts of things involving changing the timing of the milking moving the cow and the donkey farther apart in the two houses but nothing worked.  Finally, one evening the farmer decided that the problem needed divine intervention and he prayed to God that the neighbor's donkey should die.  The next morning the farmer awoke to find his cow dead.  However, this did nothing to shake the farmer's faith and he immediately bowed in prayer and said, "God, I know that you are the wise one and manage the entire universe.  One thing I can't figure out is how could you not tell apart a cow from a donkey?"

So keep up the conversation with God.  If we can add routine recitation of Gurbani to our conversations, hopefully we will get blessed with the wisdom to use our conversations for the well-being of all and keep farm animals safe around us ;)

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Waheguru simiran tips
answer:
A few keys are to:

- Learn to sit in Lotus pose for at least 15 minutes comfortably
- As mentioned, use a darker or dimly lit room
- Utilise a consistent scent in a consistent environment to condition yourself to the environment
- Get into the GAP, between thoughts of the future and anxiety and dreams about the past. The GAP is the silence that remains. Get straight into it and remain there.

question: Is getting rich bad?
answer:
Bhaji/Benji,

Getting wealthy in not against Sikhism, Guru Ji is well aware that to survive we need money. We are told to work hard, give daswandh, to prosper. Sikhs are in all areas of business and commerce and are thriving.  What is bad is when the pursuit of wealth becomes all-consuming that we forget about everything else, we forget about our spiritual journey, our reason for being here, and we just pursue money and all its trappings.

The shabad you are referring to is by Bhagat Tarlochan in which Bhagat Ji explain that we cannot leave this realm as long as we have attachments to this this world. We have many desires and longings and in our last moments if we concentrate on these desires then we are not ready to move on, we are still attached here. So in the shabad it says that if in the last moments of life we desire or remember money they we will come back to this world as a snake. If we still have attachment to our children then we come back as a pig and so on.

So work hard, earn honest pay and put some aside for daswandh and keep Guru Ji in your mind at all times and you cannot go wrong.

question: why dont farmers in punjab use plastic greenhouses
answer:
Punjab does not have plastic green-houses, but there is a similar technique that some farmers are using and the PAU (Punjab Agriculture University) “Extension Services”  is encouraging it as well. It is called Net-House Farming.  There are several reasons for recommending it over the Plastic Green houses.  One, of course, is the lower price of the nets. Also the green-house se are generally more suitable where the temperature often falls below freezing. In Punjab, that is not the major problem (except for night temperature occasionally falling to freezing point for about two weeks  - about the last week of December and middle of January). On the few days when the temperature does fall to freezing point, the dead air within the net keeps the temperature above freezing point. So there no need for complete enclosure of the green-house type.   The main problem in Punjab is the insect and pests. The net-house gives a very good protection against that.
The genetic varieties of vegetables that are suitable for growing in green-house enclosures are (generally) patented by companies. Thus to grow them, the input cost is much higher, where as in the net-houses any variety native to the area can grow as if it is growing in the open and under the local climatic condition without the attack from the pests.  Punjab has a very large genetic diversity of each vegetable that grows there.
Why is it not becoming a common practice?
 Cost of Nets is still out of reach of the  small farmers who are more likely to grow vegetables  on there small farm holdings. Also any good marketing system has not developed to pick up the produce from the farms (If produced in large quantity, quite a lot of it is likely to spoil ) and move to cities in timely fashion.

question: Looking for Advice
answer:
Dear [member],

Welcome to sikhism and this interesting discussion forum on this religion.

Most of your questions are covered by what we Sikhs refer to as Rehat Maryada (a code of conduct for Sikhs) and is available on the web at [link]

Any way as a quick reference, I will attempt to respond to some of your queries.

A Sikh is expected to marry a Sikh person. Ideally, the both partners should be Baptised (Amritdhari) Sikhs. However, practically, the two partners may be at the different stage of their path to Sikhism.

A Sikh is advised not to remove any hair from his/her body. In the past Sikhs have allowed their head (scalp)to be removed but not the hair.Again, many practising Sikhs may be in the different stage of respecting their hair. They are not banned but are encouraged to have their hair intact as they are naturally.

As per sikh religious practices the tattos would be considered 'disfiguring' the God given body so are not encoraged. However, if you have pre-existing tattos, it should not be big issue.

I hope this is of help.

Happy learning about the Sikhism as Sikh is a student all the times.

[member]

Dear [member],

Please do not misrepresent our "holy book".Nowhere is it written "that we should earn the LORD NAMES".
Almighty Lord has no one particular name.He is known by so many different names by His numerous children in this world.

Actually Gurbani teaches that we should practice the 'Name of the Lord' which in Sikhism is NAAM.This Naam has many meanings but essentially it means Essence of God.It also means sincere devotional Remembrance of God through Meditation,Simran,Kirtan,singing His Praises,etc.

Basically,Gurbani teaches us to do Naam Jap,i.e. reciting Naam(Gurmantar,Mool Mantar,Gur Shabad,...)with mouth.With practice it goes inside and becomes an 'inner' recitation.Finally it becomes 'Ajapaa Jaap' with much practice,and goes on inside the body by itself.That is when every cell('rom rom') of body is doing Naam Jap.It is a very high stage of spirituality which only Mahapurakhs(saints and Gurmukhs) attain after years of practice.Remember also that all through this process,one has to clean up bad habits of Kaam,Krodh,Lobh,Moh,Ahankaar,from one's daily routine,and live a truthful life.Then God will come to reside in the mind.Sikh then can be said to have 'merged' with Waheguru.That is the aim of human life.

Good luck and best wishes.

question: help a brother out
answer:
If you go to a new place, you will have people staring at you some times. But when you go there regularly, many of them would stop caring. After all everybody has their own life to take care of. So be humble not proud, and stay true to Guru's teachings. There is a story I would like to share:

In some tribes, there is a initiation practice of leaving a child alone in forest once he is 15. A father took his child to the tree, where he left him with his eyes blindfolded. Now the child sat beneath the tree. He knew it was already night and wild animals were prowling about. He could feel some of them really nearby. At times there were sound of something moving and a slight wind was always shaking the leaves of the tree. There was no peace and just fear with the boy. He learned to overcome it and sat bravely, waiting for it to be dawn. Soon the sun came out, the boy stood up and removed the cloth covering his eyes. He was welcomed by the morning sun. Suddenly he saw that his father was next to him. He had been sitting with his son, all the time, protecting him.

Wear your turban, follow Guru's Hukam and remember Guru Gobind Singh is always with you. It is just a matter of when he opens your eyes.

answer:
"khao" is plural or respectful use. Example: Tusi Dal Khao (you eat dal)

"kha" is singular and informal use. Example: Tun Dal Kha (you eat dal)

Also calling someone "Oye" is disrespectful unless he/she is your friend or junior. Example: Oye! Tun Dal Kha.

question: Need a couple punjabi words translated
answer:
Word 'Tanda' means a long caravan of a long distance trader laden with goods on camels or ponies. Sometimes the place where the caravans rested on a main trading route is also called Tanda. We have several villages in Punjab called Tanda. For instance, there is the 'Labana' Sikh community who had their community name derived from 'Lavan', the Sanskrit word for common salt. The Labanas were main salt trading community. This community is settled on the south side of river Beas to the north of GT Road. There is an important town Tanda in this area reminding of their caravans and resting place at Tanda.

Word 'Chog' means the act of picking of seeds and grains as their food by birds.

Tunda ('u' prononced as in tune) means a person with one hand or one arm. The word for cold is thunda ( 'th' pronounced as in the Punjabi word theek  i.e. right and 'u'' pronounced as in fund) - sometime written as thanda.

question: Jewelery and Temple
answer:
WJKK
WJKF

Like at any place of worship there are some basic proprieties that one should observe such as:
-not be inebriated or have alcohol, cigarettes upon one
-cover one’s head
-remove shoes
-wash hands before going in
-bow before the SGGS as you go in
-sit facing the SGGS with legs crossed [a bit difficult if not used to before]
-listen and pay attention to the Kirtan and accept the Prashad with due reverence.

When one goes to the Temple it is with humility, accepting that as humans we are all liable to make mistakes and asking the Lord to grant His Blessings upon us so that we can understand, obey and live as per Guru’s guidance of the Divine Command.

In my opinion any piercing whether it is of the ears, nose, lips, and eyebrows is all the same. It is just people are used to seeing women with earrings and that pierced lips and eyebrows are less common. Again there are degrees of “makeup”. Would one say that using deodorant spray is makeup?

One can get side tracked trying to split hairs. It says in SGGS:

ਪੜਿ ਪੜਿ ਪੰਡਿਤੁ ਬਾਦੁ ਵਖਾਣੈ ॥ ਭੀਤਰਿ ਹੋਦੀ ਵਸਤੁ ਨ ਜਾਣੈ ॥੩॥

The Pandits [religious scholars], read and read [Holy Scriptures] endlessly; they stir up arguments and debates [about God]; but they do not know the secret deep within [i.e. that the Lord is within all of us] ||3||

ਕਹਨ ਕਹਾਵਨ ਇਹੁ ਕੀਰਤਿ ਕਰਲਾ ॥ ਕਥਨ ਕਹਨ ਤੇ ਮੁਕਤਾ ਗੁਰਮੁਖਿ ਕੋਈ ਵਿਰਲਾ ॥੩॥

People talk on and on about Him; they consider this to be praise of God; but rare indeed is the Guru’s devotee [Gurmukh], who is above this mere talk ||3|| [virtuous living rather than mere words]

I can understand that for someone new to Sikhism, it can be bewildering as to what is acceptable and what is not. The most important thing is to seek Guru’s Sanctuary, understand His Teachings and to follow them. In short become a “Gurmukh”.

The more you understand Gurbani, you will change and things like piercing, makeup etc will not have any relevance to you anymore. So at this stage instead of worrying about these things, focus your consciousness upon the Lord.

Gur Fateh

question: ਮੈਂ ਨਹੀਂ ਸਮਝਿਆ  । (I don't understand.)
answer:
> Example: Someone is speaking to you in Punjabi language. You only speak a little Punjabi. Therefore, you say, "ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਿਓ ਜੀ । ਮੈਂ ਨਹੀਂ ਸਮਝਿਆ ਜੀ ।".
> (I'm sorry. I don't understand.)

It means "Forgive me.  I didn't understand" (applies to what was just said in a conversation happening now)

> Does "ਮੈਂ ਨਹੀਂ ਸਮਝਿਆ" (ﻣﯾں ﻧﮩﯾں ﺳﻣﺟﮭﯾﺎ) translate to "I no understood (past tense)"? Is this the best way to say, "I don't understand"?

Yes it is the best way to convey that "I didn't understand what you just said".

The proper past tense would be "main nahin samjia si", which would imply I didn't understand something that was said a while ago and we are talking about it now. to be more polite you could say "ji main nahin samjia si".

> Would it be better to say, "ਮੈਂ ਨਹੀਂ ਸਮਝਦਾ ਹਾਂ ।"?

I don't think so. It would imply "I refuse to understand" or "I don't want to understand".  Unless you specify somthing that you don't understand like "main (this matter) nahin samjada han".  It doesn't simply translate to "I don't understand". I hope that helps.

question: Samapti of Sehaj Path
answer:
[member] ji,

I can share with you the procedures I follow for samapti of sehaj path.  I hope the sangat will offer further suggestions.  I started regular daily reading of SGGS over 15 years ago.  I read five pages a day from pothis which have Gurbani as well as Punjabi and English translations provided side by side.  Once I complete one reading, I restart the new one.  I mostly follow a simple procedure, and once in a while I do follow a bit more formal procedure.  I have described both of them below.

As part of the simple procedure, I perform the Samapti usually alone using pothis.  Samapti of Sehaj Path is very similar to the beginning of path.  It includes: Reading the last page of SGGS, reciting of six stanzas of Anand Sahib (first five and the last one), performing Ardas and taking Hukamnama.  If you are restarting the reading, you can include the permission for starting the new path in the same samapti Ardas.  Alternatively, to restart path, you can recite the six Anand stanzas again, say the Ardas, take a Hukamnama and then read all or part of Japuji Sahib.

The more formal procedure involves all of the steps described above.  But the final reading is completed on installation of full SGGS Bir.  In addition, Karah Prashad is prepared and distributed and an offering is made to SGGS at the end.  The offering can be money, a rumala for the Guru or a contribution to langar.  I usually conduct the formal procedure at my local Guruduara.  Bhai Sahib ji at my local guruduara is very helpful.  I usually arrange a date with him.  The ceremony is performed immediately after the sangat leaves after morning congregation has concluded.  Karah Prashad is already available and Bhai Sahib ji helps me with the samapti.  You may be able to make an arrangement at your local guruduara.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Samapti of Sehaj Path
answer:
[member] ji,

I do not know how one would go about taking hukamnama from a laptop.  Sikh Rehat Maryada describes how hukamnama is taken from Guru Granth Sahib ji.  You open SGGS close to the middle, and read the hymn which continues at the top left of the page.  If the hymn began at the previous page, you start from the previous page.  Read the entire hymn including slok or pauri. These instructions work when reading from a book format (from SGGS Bir or separate volumes), I don't know how it should be applied while reading from a laptop.  Perhaps somebody from the sangat can advise.

In my view, the rehat (procedure) of how a shabad is selected for hukamnama is less important, instead our primary objective is to contemplate and follow the selected shabad.  With this in mind, you have the following options:
1.  Go to your local guruduara or somebody's house where SGGS is installed, and take the hukamnama as per rehat.
2.  There is an option for cyber hukamnama at this link:  [link]
3.  Adopt today's hukamnama from Sri Darbar Sahib Amritsar available at http://www.sikhnet.com/hukam-orig as hukam for you and contemplate on this shabad
4.  Go to around page 700 of SGGS on your laptop, and then randomly hit page down a few times, and read the shabad continuing at even page number.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh

question: Any Sikh writing for Anger management ?
answer:
[member] Ji,

Unfortunately, there is no easy solution or remedy that can help in anger control. I have known plenty of people who recite baani and still are very angry. My own grandfather woke up 4:00am in the morning and did path for 2 hours every day, was vegetarian, etc and was the angriest man I have known. My father, who occasionally does path, eats meat, but is the most serene man I have ever met. It’s more about applying the teachings of Sikhi in your life and not merely reciting baani or vegetarianism. From my personal experience, I have noticed that people who are humble tend to have less anger. Sikh Teachings really emphasise the importance of humility. To start with, I would ask you to really honestly look at yourself and see what triggers your anger.

The fact that you are asking this question on this forum is a great first step because it solidifies that you have acknowledged the problem. Realization of the problem is always the best first step to resolving it.

question: Women's Hair
answer:
Dear [member]

Congratulations on your 'conversion' in January!  I hope you are realising Guruji's Kirpa in your life.  Sorry to hear you have encountered trouble at your workplace.

When you say you converted, did you make a conscious decision to become a Sikh and live the lifestyle, or did you become Amritdhari?

If you are starting out as a Sikh, you are not obliged to keep your head covered, but it is highly recommended as you get further along the path towards receiving amrit.  The head covering can be a scarf (chunni/dupatta), a bandanna, a head wrap (there are plenty of styles on YouTube) or the traditional turban.  Don't feel that you must wear a turban at this stage (although it is the ultimate goal).

It would be Sikhs who have not received amrit (become 'baptised') who you have seen with their heads uncovered.

Sikhs who have become amrit shak must keep their heads covered, the bare minimum being when in public, but I believe most keep their heads covered for the majority of the time (some even sleep with their keskis on).  Amritdhari men must wear a turban (per the Sikh Rehat Maryada) and women have the choice to wear a turban or some other head covering.  For the purposes of unity, equality and connection to Guru Sahibans, the turban for all Sikhs would be best.

If you are not amritdhari you have the choice to cover your head or not, in whichever circumstances you are in.  Relationships with local Sikhs in your area may also help you gain strength and certainty in your practices.

May Guruji guide you in your dilemma.

question: What do you call the mat/rug in langar?
answer:
Tappar used to be very common in school class rooms in India/Pakistan where desks were not available. The material, of which the Tapparwas made used to be similar in texture to what we see in the Langar. Another reason for it to be called Tappar is its dimensions that are similar to the classroom mats. That is it is about 2ft wide and can be fairly long may be 20 to 30ft. On the other hand a durrie is mostly woven from cotton thread mainly and has coloured woven patterns and the dimensions resemble those of usual beds or rooms where the durrie is spread out. For practical reasons of difficulty of washing durries being made from  cotton and not being water proof makes them unsuitable for Langar floors. The mat or Tappar these days is made of synthetic materials and is relatively easy to clean. Above all, the mat or Tappar dimensions are suitable for sitting to eat in a line on the floor.

question: The Reason for the attachment?
answer:
Bhenji,
We are sent to this world because of unfinished business. We have unfinished karma that we need to work through so we come here.
One question that some major faiths find difficult to answer – A child is born, takes one breath and dies, explain.
This whole system is so so intricate that we have no idea of it. We meet people we leave people. We have little incidents when we go out shopping of instance, we may bump into someone, we may have an argument with someone over a parking space, our shopping bag may snap and some good person may come along and help us gather the things up. Sometime we think “what a nice person that was” or “what a nasty self-centred person that was”, but in the end we just pass it off as one of those things. In fact what is happening is we are working through our karma, every little insy winsy teeny weeny bit of it, but we do not realize it. When something happens and we react with good intensions then we work off the bad karma and increase the good, if we react badly then we increase our bad. Every action, , every curse, every blessing, very look, every thought is debited or credited to our account. It happens 24/7.
It is no coincidence that you work with the people you work with, it is no coincidence you have the friends you have or the enemies you have. In the same way it is no coincidence you have the pets you have. We bought the kids a kitten, a lovely light ginger one with white paws and a white face. When they come home the first thing they do is go up to the cat (its now grown up) pick it up, cuddle it and basically treat it like it was some little baby, we find ourselves doing the same thing, I talk baby-talk with it!  The thing is this soul, in the form of a cat in this life, is someone close to us from a previous existence, he has come back and we love it because that connection from before is still there. Who knows who this cat is to us (only Guru knows) but we treat it like part of the family, we realize that there is connection so in our ardaas we ask GuruJi to give mukhti to this soul as well.

In the same way, although you hated cats/dogs, the circle of karma is too strong, you had to work your way through it, you had to look after that dog, and due to your previous connection to it that love appeared, there was no way you could have fought against it. You took take of it, cleaned its mess and when the time came for him to go, he went. Be thankful that you took care of it, he was happy and he has gone hopefully to a better place. If you like do an akhand path for him, or a langar in his name and he will get the benefit, where ever he is.

question: ਮੇਰਿਆਂ ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਾਨ
answer: I am no expert in Punjabi grammer but it was my first language.  So from a spoken Punjabi perspective, "Maire" sounds more natural to my ear in this sentence than "Mairean", which you don't hear being used so often.  Hope that helps.

extra.question_body:
ਮੇਰਿਆਂ ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਾਨ

Can someone confirm if the grammer is correct. I have provided an explanation for the inflectional forms.

My country men's pride.

ਮੇਰਿਆਂ = special inflected form of masc. pl. ਮੇਰੇ when it is followed by a postposition. In this example ਮੇਰੇ is part of a "noun phrase" followed by a postposition. This is why ਮੇਰੇ is replaced with ਮੇਰਿਆਂ.

ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ = pl. form irr. masc n. (and adj.) "ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀ" (country man > country men)

ਦੀ = postposition "of" when it proceeds a sg. fem. n.
ਸ਼ਾਨ = pride (sg. fem. n.)

question: ਮੇਰਿਆਂ ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਾਨ
answer: [member], very good reply. I think grammatically, I might have it correct. However, I don't think too many Punjabi speakers follow that "if followed by a postposition" rule. I think most would expect me to say ਮੇਰੇ (whether it is grammatically correct or not).

question: ਮੇਰਿਆਂ ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਾਨ
answer:
Waheguru ji ka khalsa
Waheguru ji ki fateh

In the case of ਮੇਰਿਆਂ ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਾਨ the possessive plural word ਮੇਰਿਆਂ is IMHO not appropriate grammatically. The appropriate word should have been ਮੇਰੇ. The form of the possessive word is decided by the number category of the word immediately following the possessive word. Thus the sentence in Punjabi meaning the ‘language of people ofmy village ’ would be ‘ਮੇਰੇ ਪਿੰਡ ਦੇ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਦੀ ਬੋਲੀ’. And to say the ‘ language of people of my villages’ would be  ‘ਮੇਰਿਆਂ ਪਿੰਡਾਂ ਦੇ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਦੀ ਬੋਲੀ’. Therfore, the correct phrase should be ‘ਮੇਰੇ ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਾਨ.
Humbly

ਮੇਰਿਆਂ ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਾਨ

Can someone confirm if the grammer is correct. I have provided an explanation for the inflectional forms.

My country men's pride.

ਮੇਰਿਆਂ = special inflected form of masc. pl. ਮੇਰੇ when it is followed by a postposition. In this example ਮੇਰੇ is part of a "noun phrase" followed by a postposition. This is why ਮੇਰੇ is replaced with ਮੇਰਿਆਂ.

ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀਆਂ = pl. form irr. masc n. (and adj.) "ਦੇਸ਼ ਵਾਸੀ" (country man > country men)

ਦੀ = postposition "of" when it proceeds a sg. fem. n.
ਸ਼ਾਨ = pride (sg. fem. n.)

extra.question_body:
Waheguru ji ka khalsa Waheguru ji ki fateh ||

One basic question: Do I have to take out daswand (10% of my gross/net income) if i am paying tax to the government of the country i live in. The idea of Daswand is to contribute to the society, or people in need and not to be sticky with Money.

Tax is collected for the citizens of the country and is a pool of money used for all of us together. the poor are given more than riches and eventually used of the similar purpose.

Daswand looks more like DIY (Do-it-yourself) utilization of money for the good of society whereas tax is for betterment of the  country's infrastructure / help needy citizens with more benefits etc and is more managed by the government (just like an investment manager in financial domain).

I am confused if i am carrying forward this concept of daswand just as a ritual without giving a thought that government collect the tax for the similar purpose and i am paying 30% of my gross income into taxes. Even if a third of that money goes to the poors or needy citizens, my job to take out the daswand is done already.

What are your thoughts?
